utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Ciaglinski.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Your cross-examination by Mr. Petrovic will continue. Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ciaglinski, I would like to come back to the point in fact where we left off on Friday. You told us in the course of your testimony on Friday that there existed some higher level of the commission for cooperation in Belgrade, and after that I asked you why you were mentioning that for the first time, and this is what you answered: [In English] "I am somewhat surprised because I speak about what I know but I believe that others have spoken about what they know and it has been discussed in their evidence." [Interpretation] That's transcript page 6865. Could you please tell us who are those others that testified about this, that you know of.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can well imagine that as I was taking part in this, the trial of Mr. Milosevic, I often used to read the transcripts which were published on the ICTY web site. And somewhere in those readings and of my general sort of knowledge of how things worked, I was aware that there was a higher level representation in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Could you then clarify what is your memory of the events versus what you read from the transcripts and heard in the testimony of others. How, more importantly, will we be able to distinguish between your personal knowledge and the second-hand knowledge that you gained from the media, the listening to the hearings, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, from my personal knowledge I know that General Bo Pelmas was in Belgrade and his job was to be the main conduit or a conduit of our contact with Belgrade. So I am aware of that, and I did meet General Bo Pelmas on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ciaglinski, on Friday you did not tell us this is what I know and this is what I heard from others. All that you have told us, both about the commission and other topics, you represented as your personal knowledge, your own memory. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly what I told you was from my own personal knowledge, and over seven years since the last trial, five, six, seven years, whatever the last time was, you know, I have discussed, I have read, and it's very difficult to remember exactly what was exactly my personal knowledge and what is -- what I've read about and heard and discussed. But in general, I would say that my knowledge was that Bo Pelmas was our representative in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thus you cannot make a clear distinction for us between what you personally know and what you know from the transcripts and the newspapers. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Hold on, please, there's an objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we specify what we're talking about. Are we talking about every single statement in his statement or a particular item? I think it's an unfair question, if he's addressing it to everything that was in his written statement. We need to go item by item, otherwise it's a compound, complex question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, to what are you directing this point? Is it everything the witness has said or is it one particular subject?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I started my examination today with a very specific topic, the issue of the commission, that is the higher representation that the witness has mentioned. Further answers of the witness went in the direction, indicating that all that he has said relies both on his personal knowledge and what he has read. So that does go to his testimony in general, but I will try to refocus and come back to what we've started with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Petrovic, I don't think you can draw from the evidence so far that the witness was saying in regard to what I said on Friday, I can't now tell you how much was personal knowledge and how much is from what I've read. He is saying that there are circumstances in which it is difficult to disentangle the two, and if you want to make a point of that, I'm afraid you'll have to go into the detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will try to do that, Your Honour, through specific questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So let us come back to the issue of the commission, or rather, the various levels of the commission of which you said on Friday, if I'm not mistaken, that you were first asked about it on Friday by me. And that was why you first answered to that issue on Friday. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have an objection here, too, because if the question just refers to the commission, we need some clarification whether we're talking about the commission in Pristina, that this witness was a participant in; or the commission in Belgrade; or some other level of the commission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, I think that level -- that question was clear. It was the issue of whether there were more than one level that Mr. Petrovic directed his question to, and the witness has agreed that the first time that that arose in his evidence was in answer to cross-examination by Mr. Petrovic. So let's -- that question's been answered. We can move to the next one.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I may say, it's not exactly my recollection, but that may well be the case now the witness has answered it. I did think it arose in the evidence in chief, but that can only be checked later.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, maybe I can help you. On page 6866, on Friday, there is a passage which I quoted loosely, but I hope the witness does not mind. I don't think this is in dispute. If you allow me, I will ask my next question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ciaglinski, with all due respect, I believe that what you told us, both today and on Friday, namely that you were first asked about various levels of the commission, is simply not true. And why am I saying that? On page 3276 of the transcript of the Milosevic trial, Slobodan Milosevic explicitly asked you about the federal commission, and you said this: [In English] "The only commission that I knew was the commission headed by Loncar in Pristina. That was the level that I worked with." [Interpretation] So to Milosevic's question about the federal commission you answered there was one commission you know of and that is the one that worked on your level in Pristina; I think that is a bit different from what you are telling us today and what you told us on Friday. You said there was one commission in Milosevic's time and now you're talking about two different levels of the same commission or even two different commissions. Could you explain the difference between your testimony here and your testimony in the Milosevic trial, if you can, of course.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I can. Memory has a habit of playing tricks on you, and if you actually continued to read the transcript of the Milosevic trial, you will find a section where it says: Do you know who General Pelmas was? Which then triggered my memory and I think I said the same to the words of the effect: Do you mean Bo Pelmas? So at the time -- it had totally slipped my mind and that's why I didn't actually remember about the commission at the higher level, but once it was -- when Pelmas's name was mentioned, it came back.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: But in the course of that testimony you did not correct your prior statement. You didn't say there existed a commission at a higher level and a commission at a lower level, my level in Pristina. That is not in the transcript, and if I am mistaken I stand to be corrected. Yes, Bo Pelmas was mentioned, but nothing was said about the existence of two different levels of the commission or even two different commissions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not sure about that. I would ask counsel to read to the witness the continuing section of the Milosevic transcript --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The page, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was at the bottom of the page that he just cited, 3276, where the witness is reminded about Bo Pelmas, the Swedish general, beginning at line 23 and continuing on to the next question and answer on the following page.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, is it necessary for me to read that? If it is, I would appreciate a moment to find the passage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I think if you go over the page you'll see the answer the witness gave. The question Milosevic put at the top of page 3277.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. The answer was -- here, Your Honour. If necessary, I can read the whole passage. So the witness is answering to the question that I asked: [In English] "The only commission I knew," [No interpretation], [In English] "And General Bo Pelmas who also communicated on behalf of your mission with headquarters in Belgrade, [No interpretation], [In English] I have no idea who General Bo Pelmas is. This is the first time I heard his name." [Interpretation] Then again [In English] "Swedish general who was also your representative in Belgrade and he communicated with the government in Belgrade. Sorry, Bo Pelmas, yes, sorry, I misunderstood the pronunciation. I did see him. He was working in Belgrade. He was our representative to government in Belgrade. He communicated with the commission headquarters in Belgrade. Absolutely right." [Interpretation] I don't see, Your Honour, with all due respect that from that we can conclude that the witness was talking about two levels of the commission or two commissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, my learned friend apparently failed to read the phrase "this commission that was set up by the Federal Government."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: He did fail to read it, but there's no reason why he can't cross-examine on this, Mr. Hannis, and we'll get it sorted out by the witness if he wishes to continue with his examination on this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think, Your Honour, that the transcript is self-explanatory. I will not dwell anymore on it. I think it's clear that what he said today and on Friday is very different from what he said in 2001, and I think that makes clear my point. I'll move on. Could we show --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could I just ask you one other question. Is one of your points that there was no commission in Belgrade? Let's get to the meat of this. Is there an issue over whether or not there was a commission in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the state of affairs will soon be clarified. There was only one commission, and I was just intending to put an exhibit before the witness, a Defence exhibit, that I believe will shed appropriate light on your question. So can the witness be shown the English version of 2D8.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ciaglinski, do you have it in front of you, 2D8?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... No. I'll try on my glasses. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's on its way.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Here we are.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Would you kindly look at this document. It is very short, and then I would like to ask you a couple of questions about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we scroll down a bit so the witness can see the whole page and the second page as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Have you seen the second page? I can't really see what you are seeing, Mr. Ciaglinski.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I've only seen the first page so far.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the second page shown as well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Have you read it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can we agree, Mr. Ciaglinski, that this is a document whereby the Federal Government of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia sets up the commission for cooperation with the OSCE?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: So it appears. I've never seen this document before, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Could you look please look at page 1 again, para 2, of this decision. In that paragraph 2, the tasks of the commission are defined. Can you tell us whether the tasks of the commission defined in this way are consistent with your perception of the affairs of which the commission you cooperated with was in charge?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because this is the higher level commission, and the commission I dealt with was the cooperation commission in Pristina, which was the working level commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you stand by your claim that General Loncar headed this commission that you dealt with?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The person in charge of the commission and who portrayed himself as in charge of the organisation in Pristina was General Loncar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness please be shown 2D9.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Please look through this document, Mr. Ciaglinski. This document is an amendment to the previous decision. Based on this document, would you accept my assertion that General Loncar was one of the members of the commission but certainly not the chairman of the commission or the chairman of a separate commission that existed in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I've seen, it is quite apparent that General Loncar was a member of the commission; however, he was the representative of that commission in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't believe the witness can help us any more with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ciaglinski. I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But, Your Honour, I hope --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I hope that with these two documents I have managed to explain our position on the issue of how many commissions there were, whether there was a lower level and a higher level commission, and I hope at least our position and the facts are clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, if it helps, I can indicate the picture I have at the moment, and that is that there is a supervisory body set up at federal level, but they've got to get down to work with the OSCE and deal with day-to-day events on the ground. What the witness has described to us is the operational element of the commission, whether it's 1 or 2 or 22, but the operational level in Kosovo on the ground seemed to him, from his experience, to be headed by General Loncar. And I don't see anything inconsistent with that and what's set out in these two documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I quite understand that this witness cannot tell us any more about it and I have no intention of asking him any further questions. I just wanted to confront him with these documents and now I'll move on other questions. Your Honour, my colleague tells me that the record does not show that this last document we've seen was 2D9.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that has now been corrected. Thank you, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ciaglinski, I would now like to briefly take up this meeting of the 16th of January -- 6th of January.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: That you mentioned. Let us remind ourselves of what you said on Friday; namely, that some major issues were discussed at that meeting, convened on the 6th of January. And on pages 6829 and 6830 of Friday's transcript, you spoke about what those issues were, the problem with the helicopter, the KLA prisoners held in the prison in Nis. First of all, I would like to ask you about those prisoners in Nis. When did you receive permission to visit them? After you presented that problem at the meeting, when did you actually receive the permission to see them in their detention in Nis?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was several days later, maybe seven, eight, nine, ten days.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So you did not receive any approval at that moment; the approval came ten days later. That's what we read in your statement, among other things.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what happened was that Mr. Sainovic said that it would be arranged, but there had to be procedures followed for the arrangement to be made.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Right. And actually, from your perspective, you don't know what the procedures were, who gave approvals and what kind of approvals were necessary. All you know is that at some point within ten days, General Loncar called you up and told you, Mr. Ciaglinski, you can now visit the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think during the meeting Mr. Sainovic did mention that judges would have to be consulted and the judiciary would, obviously, have to comment on it. However, because the whole thing was part of a deal to release the soldiers, it was a foregone conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: But you received formal approval ten days later?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You also mentioned that at that meeting of the 6th of January, Sainovic said something also about the relationship of the mission and the KLA, or the attitude of the mission towards the KLA. I would like to ask you a couple questions about that. First of all, since I see that you followed this trial and probably other trials before this Tribunal, do you know that there is a significant number of Albanian witnesses who claim that the Kosovo Liberation Army, in the period of your stay in Kosovo and during the tenure of the mission in Kosovo, they availed themselves of this opportunity to re-arm and reinforce their troops? Did you hear such testimony?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think more to the point, I mean, I actually was aware that this was happening on the ground. I didn't have to avail myself of the testimony; I saw it happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I will very briefly put before you part of the testimony of a person who testified before this Chamber, Bislim Zyrapi, who was head of staff of the KLA up to March 1998. In answer to one of my colleagues from one of the Defence teams, from November 1998 to March 1999, that man was Chief of the General Staff of the KLA. It's page 6020. He was asked whether it was immediately after that, in October, November, December -- he was asked, in fact, whether it was fair to say that the KLA used this period to consolidate and regroup their forces, and the head of the KLA said, Yes, we used that time to consolidate. Further on, on page 6180, the same witness answers questions about how many members of the KLA were on the ground in March 1999; mentions 17 to 18.000 KLA soldiers. So my first question, and, in fact, you confirmed this before; namely, that you agree that the KLA used your presence to consolidate themselves militarily in Kosovo. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure that they used our presence, but they did consolidate in that period, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Tell us, please, the documents that governed your presence in Kosovo, did they envisage some specific obligations with regard to the units and members of the Kosovo Liberation Army? Were there any restrictions regarding their number on the ground, their deployment on the ground, the level of their arming? Were there any such elements in the documents governing your mission in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In documents governing your presence in Kosovo and Metohija, was KLA limited as to the number and types of weapons on ammunition supplies or supply of new weapons? Were there any restrictions with that regard and with regards to the KLA?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But I believe that Christopher Hill, an American diplomat, was in constant negotiation with the KLA and the OSCE were forever trying to tell them to -- not to do what they were doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: The OSCE tried to recommend that there was no obligation imposed to the KLA during the presence of the verification mission in Kosovo; is it true?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Geremek agreement, there was no reference at all to the restrictions placed upon the KLA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, that's the same question asked three times, as I read it, or am I missing something? You got a really good answer the first time I thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Your Honour, I agree with you. I don't want to enter into arguments. There are certain nuances, but I agree and I'm going to move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ciaglinski, apart from your presence enabled what we are discussing right now, was there any active attitude or relationship between your mission and the KLA in terms of specific and concrete help to the KLA in certain aspects of their activities?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not aid the KLA in any of their activities. We were purely trying to get them to be reasonable and not to re-arm and not to attack the legitimate forces of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You said on Friday that you once or on more occasions met Commander Remi, one of the regional or zonal commanders of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, by your leave, I would like to play a short segment from the BBC's documentary, The Fall of Milosevic, where Commander Remi explains the nature of their relationship with the mission and the consequences of such relationship to their activities on the ground. If it pleases the Bench, it will take up to one and a half minutes, and I will have placed into the e-court a transcript of that documentary, 2D7, and pages 42, 43, 44 on e-court. So by your leave, we would like to play this to the witness and we would like to elicit his comments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The -- what is the source of the transcript that you say you've given to the booth?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Prosecution submitted a transcribed documentary, the whole broadcast -- the whole programme, The Fall of Milosevic, has been transcribed, and I've highlighted those pages that are of interest to us in this -- at this point. So we can follow the transcript concurrently with the playback, with the video, because it's all in English, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand the purpose of this. Now, Mr. Hannis, what is the source of this transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This we received from the BBC. This is the BBC version, the script to the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So what we will have is the KLA commander speaking Albanian and a transcript. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think it's undertitled in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, can I tell you that -- and I thought I had raised this before. This may be the first time we've had an excerpt from this documentary in this trial, but in the Milosevic trial on a number of occasions the subtitles were shown to be inaccurate in this documentary. It's a tendentious piece of work in a number of respects, and we have been very cautious with it. And I had hoped that a proper translation of this was going to be done, Mr. Hannis. Was that not raised in the pre-trial stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We talked about that, Your Honour, but we're not offering this. If we were offering it, we would provide a translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, but it's still the original transcript that's with Mr. Petrovic. So what I'm going to do is ask the interpreters to do their best to avoid the use of the guiding transcript as far as possible; and if possible, to give us a translation as they hear it. Now, I know it's difficult in a situation where the witness is probably speaking very quickly, but hopefully that's what will emerge. Carry on, please, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I would like the video to be played to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: "The balance of power in Kosovo was about to shift. "[Voiceover]: [No interpretation]. "[No interpretation]. We tried to make use of the agreement to bring supplies and to open new channels of communication."

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the first part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Stop there. I got virtually no translation of that, possibly because of the difficulty of dealing with it, and therefore I'm relying at the moment on the subtitles. Plainly, they are satisfactory for your purpose, and I suspect this is a passage in which these subtitles are fairly accurate. But it's strikes me you're asking yet again a question to which you've already had a clear answer, particularly from Mr. Zyrapi. And I'm concerned about why you're not content to accept his figures and his account of events, since he was a Prosecution witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, by your leave, of course that -- this is not contentious. Zyrapi is talking about passive assistance provided by the OSCE mission to the KLA. Commander Remi goes a step forward. This is not just a passive attitude that facilitates their growth and development. He speaks about active cooperation and support that he enjoys from the OSCE mission, and this is my point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, please go on with your questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us now play back the second part of this segment, some tens or 20-odd seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: "I was thinking that we had somehow, were leaning in the opposite direction. "Some of the monitors did lean and mostly one way. "[Voiceover] The assistance we received is something which helped us to find out our bearings and things which are helpful to every army. It is normal the Americans and the British help us most. "[No interpretation]."

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I now move on to asking a number of questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: First, sir, I am -- whether this person - I don't mean President Chirac, I mean Commander Remi, was that the person you met on several occasions or once in 1998/1999?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The person that was subtitled to be Remi was indeed Remi who I met with a group of others several times, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Commander Remi states several examples of assistance on the part of the Americans and the British provided to his side in the conflict. Does Commander Remi paint a true picture of the state of affairs on the ground or not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The impression I had from what he said and from the subtitles was that the presence and sort of the cease-fire in Kosovo had allowed these reinforcements and re-arming, but I don't remember at any point that he said the OSCE had any part to play in this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Let me read out to you page 43. Let us not go back to the video. It's easier to read this on the transcript. So it's page 43, otherwise it's known as 2D7, and Remi says: [In English] "They were just what we needed. Every enemy -- every army needs them to get coordinated right. Of course it was the Americans and the British who helped us." [Interpretation] That is more than passively observing what was going on, at least in my opinion.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea what "get coordinated right" means. It means nothing to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When one warring party gets supplied with maps that may be used in their efforts against the other party in a conflict, does this mean anything to you; and this was specifically what he was referring to?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you are referring to the maps that the KVM were using, the maps were not very brilliant anyway, but in order to make sure that we were talking from the same hymn sheet, from the same coordinates, there probably were maps given to the KLA, as maps were given to the Serbian side as well, the same maps. And these maps were never very good, and that's why we eventually asked them, requested them, were given your maps to use, which we did not pass on to anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: But those maps were evidently a significant help to one of the parties in the conflict, at least in accordance with what this man said on video?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think his comment about "get coordinated right," I know coordinated -- there's another word "coordinates" therefore implies maps. But I don't think he's talking about maps at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the interpretation that we had, for what it's worth in the circumstances, did not use maps, it used information. But again it was done in circumstances which are not entirely helpful. And of course a point of view is being made by this programme. It's like this all the way through, whether it's one side or the other it's dealing with. That's the impression I have, without saying that that's the entirety of the programme. So, Mr. Petrovic, if this -- if -- and this applies to everyone. If there's going to be another occasion when this programme or any other of a similar nature is to be used as part of the evidence, then we will require a CLSS translation of the dialogue to be -- to accompany the viewing of the film, otherwise there is going to be this ongoing difficulty with interpretation. And so far as this one is concerned, the Trial Chamber orders you to get a CLSS translation of the two clips that you've actually shown so that we can then reflect the witness's answers against what was actually said in the documentary.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am going to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So on the basis of a handful of facts that we dwelled upon and the first fact was that at the very least the KLA used the presence of the Kosovo Verification Mission to strengthen their ranks and regroup, where does in this context you find the dissatisfaction of the Serbian side with the developments on the ground? And can you understand their reasons and some of the reasons of their dissatisfaction with the developments on the ground together with your presence in the relevant period that we are discussing?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can tell you that some of the assumptions made about their reinforcement are also interesting because there was no reduction of forces on the border. And the only places that the weapons are coming across were across the border; they were not being flown in or driven in. They were coming across on the back of mules. Now, there was no reduction of the Serbian forces and the Serbian forces were carrying out daily operations. I can understand, and this is -- the dissatisfaction was mentioned often to us in meetings at -- while the VJ troops are sitting in the barracks, it was allowing the KLA to repossess various positions and various trench lines around Kosovo; that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Good. I have some other questions for you. In your statement on paragraph -- on page 5, paragraph 6 in the English version of course, you mentioned that Sainovic was speaking on behalf of the Federal Government in Belgrade when it concerned certain issues of interest to you. Do you know that at the time we are discussing that Mr. Sainovic was vice-president of the government of the Federal Government, and that would be only natural for him to speak on the -- on behalf of the Federal Government? Would that be natural to you to know that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You mean it would be illogical for a vice-president of the army to speak on behalf of the government where he is vice-president?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The answer was the opposite, Mr. Petrovic. It was the natural thing to expect him to speak on behalf of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, yes. Of course. It was interpreted differently to me but I find it satisfactory. Thank you. I am going to try to shorten my questioning. Only a few questions more.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: On several occasions you mentioned that as time went by General Loncar would visit to Belgrade -- visit Belgrade more frequently for consultations and that he did not attend the meetings in Pristina. Can you personally testify to the fact with whom General Loncar spoke in Belgrade when he would be absent from Pristina? Could you testify personally to that effect?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't with him, so how could I know?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that General Loncar became a member of the cooperation commission with the OSCE mission at the direct insistence of Slobodan Milosevic? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought it was more complicated than that, and I thought it was because William Walker actually had previous experience with General Loncar from another area in the Balkans, but I bow to your knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that at meetings with Milosevic, your meeting on the 6th of January, 1999, there were certain demands that were expressed. One of them was the visit to the Nis detention, then the helicopter issue, and the fuel issue. Is it true --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 22, line 10, it doesn't say meetings with Milosevic, we mean meetings with Sainovic. This is an obvious mistake in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So is it true that the issue of the prisoners was dealt with satisfactorily in accordance with your demands? Is it true that the issue of fuel was subsequently and very soon was dealt with satisfactorily, in accordance with your demands?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are two questions there. Can we have one at a time?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that response or reply to both questions would be the same; but if not, Mr. Ciaglinski will correct me. I can, of course, go one by one, but I'm trying to be as through with this cross as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Bearing in mind there are two issues there, Mr. Ciaglinski, could you address them separately, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. In relation to the prisoners, we had an undertaking that that problem would be resolved and the meetings would be arranged, and the fuel problem did improve and our fuel supplies increased, but not everywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: My last question for you concerns the third issue that you broached on that meeting and it goes for the helicopters. It is true that the Serbian and Yugoslav side offered you a VJ helicopter that would be painted white bearing the International Red Cross's symbol. Is it true that this was the proposal of the Yugoslav and Serb side to you, representatives of the OSCE mission?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Geremek agreement had allowed for unlimited access to our aircraft, and we had an aircraft on stand-by the whole time --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Ciaglinski. This is a simple question. Give us a simple answer. So for medevac purposes, did the Yugoslav and Serbian side offer you a white-painted helicopter bearing International Red Cross symbol to be placed at your disposal, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We could not use the helicopter that was similar to the ones that your forces used for attacking the KLA, which was a well-known model. And therefore, yes, you are quite right we were offered that; we could not accept it for our own safety reasons and for the safety of our verifiers. It's very difficult to actually distinguish on a foggy day whether it's a military helicopter bearing a white cross or whether it's a military aircraft flying in to attack you, but you can distinguish the type and the sound of the helicopter very easily.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is the reference to the prisoners a reference to Serb soldiers who had been taken prisoner?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir. The --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Or I --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the KLA who had been imprisoned back in December.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, and you've referred to these, I think, 11 KLA prisoners. But you in an earlier answer said that the visit was tied up with the release of soldiers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: These were the Serb soldiers who had been taken by the KLA. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't think we went into detail, or perhaps I missed the detail, but it is a subject that has arisen in another context. The one other matter, Mr. Petrovic, I would like to deal with is the translation of the transcript -- or the provision of a transcript of any similar film. The matter did arise at a 65 ter conference on the 21st of June, where it was said that where any party wanted to rely on particularly interviews from the Death of Yugoslavia or The Fall of Milosevic, translation should be obtained well in advance of the evidence being presented, and that meant official translations from this institution or another acceptable institution - there are many places you can get the translation - which the Defence could stipulate to. And the point was being made, I think, to the Prosecution, but it was also made whenever anybody wants to rely on this, that's what should happen. So I think it appropriate to reiterate that and make it now an order that unless that happens, these interviews will be skipped here rather than presented in an unsatisfactory way. And as far as today's is concerned, you can resolve the matter by obtaining the transcript that we've asked you to do. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if you allow me, I relied with full confidence on the transcript provided by the BBC itself, but I did compare what the BBC provided in a written document and what is really pronounced in the English translation and I thought that was satisfactory for the second passage. But in every following situation, we will of course require a translation from the CLSS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Ciaglinski. My name is Djuro Cepic, attorney-at-law. I have a couple of questions for you. We heard earlier today and on Friday that you attended almost 90 per cent of meetings held between the commission of the Federal Government on one hand and the Kosovo Verification Mission, of which you were a member, on the other hand. I'm interested in meetings between the KVM and the representatives of the Pristina Corps. I have information that there were 101 such meetings. You attended a certain number of them, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Among other things, on the 4th of May -- sorry, the 4th of March, you accepted mediation or you accepted to mediate in the release of a soldier whose uncle and father had been previously killed in the municipality of Vucitrn. Milan Mitrovic is the name of the soldier. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Similarly, you briefed the other side at these meetings that there was a high risk of KLA terrorist operations, wherein they would place explosive devices in urban environments. Did you do that? Such a meeting was held on the 5th of March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to understand the question, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I'll try to rephrase it and make it clearer. On the 5th of March, 1999, there was a meeting you attended, and at that meeting information was given that there is a chance that terrorists, members of the KLA, might place bombs in large towns and cities. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll move on to Podujevo. On the 26th of December, 1998, terrorists killed at his own doorstep the last Serb who lived in Podujevo, Milo Radojevic. After that incident, in talking to officers of the Army of Yugoslavia you said that it was a heinous crime, classic terrorism, and you commended the Army of Yugoslavia on their professional conduct. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What I'm interested in is this: Apart from these meetings, you also toured positions of the Army of Yugoslavia. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On Friday in the course of your testimony you mentioned that you visited three most important positions of the Army of Yugoslavia and you named the locations. Can you tell me why precisely those three positions were the most vital in the eyes of your mission?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. When I said "vital," these were the three positions that were in one of the original agreements. They were company positions [realtime transcript read in error "accompanied"], the large positions, and the commanding a large territory from their positions. They were high -- they commanded communications, they had good views and visibility, so -- and we had trouble for some time being able to get into those areas, but eventually a highly organised visit to these locations was organised and allowed us to see all we wanted to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Are you aware, Mr. Ciaglinski, that before your visit those same units that you mentioned were also visited by the Kosovo Diplomatic Observers Mission, KDOM, in the month of October, and this inspection gave rise to no objections whatsoever. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was before I arrived, so I can't confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Just one more question about the KDOM. Do you know, perhaps, since at that moment you were not in Kosovo, that that mission conducted a large number of verifications and inspections, especially of anti-aircraft weaponry? And again, they had no comments, no objections.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've seen reports of that, yes, which I read in Pristina. Can I just say that there was a mistake, sir. In line 14, 15:19:36 which it says "they were accompanied positions," they were company positions, as in companies of infantry or companies of troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that. On Friday you said that you encountered problems when you wanted to tour barracks or military installation without prior announcement, and the same occurred when you tried to visit a unit in the border area. As an officer you should know, Mr. Ciaglinski, that especially in the border belt, due to security measures, because of possible ambushes and patrols of the army, all visits had to be announced 24 hours earlier and one had to be accompanied by a liaison officer. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not entirely correct, no, because the actual agreement states that if we wish to visit a military unit on the border belt, that was the procedure; but they -- also in a document it does say that we have full freedom of movement and access, and that must include the border belt itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Well, you did visit the border belt and conducted verifications there, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Often with great difficulty, and towards the end not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you aware that there was an agreed procedure, agreed among the regional centres of the Kosovo Verification Mission and the garrisons of the Army of Yugoslavia, whereby the 3rd Army prescribed that the presence of a liaison officer from the Army of Yugoslavia was indispensable?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I, in fact, helped draft and disseminate that order to our units. But this was in March, this was when the situation was becoming very grave and very dangerous and it was thought to be a sensible way to carry out our work in the border belt.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Similarly, on the 24th of January, 1999, or, rather, a team of the Kosovo Verification Mission headed by you visited Junik, a place north-west of Pristina. And there you talked to local ethnic Albanians, who told you they experienced no problems with members of the VJ, and you also visited a VJ unit there. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember if I was actually accompanied by Colonel Kotur when I visited Junik, so that's what they did say. And I also visited a VJ unit, yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the course of your testimony on Friday you said that the VJ would usually use for their drills, which were allowed under the agreement, surfaces of 10 by 10 kilometres or even 20 by 20 kilometres. You also said you knew very well that the area next to the air-field south of Podujevo was an old practicing ground for the Army of Yugoslavia. Do you know of any other such grounds that the Army of Yugoslavia used; and if you do, can you tell us which are they?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a question we often asked, to which we were never given an answer where the training areas really were. But, for example, I imagine there was a training area quite close to Prizren, near the barracks, and the regional centres might have known better because they were actually on the ground in those regions. But in general, I was told that the Yugoslav army could train where it wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: In your statement you mentioned that at that time the army significantly increased the number of its garrisons. Can you tell us as an officer, what is a garrison?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's -- obviously, it's semantics where a garrison is a fixed location where there are a large number of troops with support facilities. We probably -- well, I should have maybe say it is -- that they increased -- is it the number of troops in the garrisons, did I say, or they increased the number of garrisons? I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: You said the number of garrisons. And what would you say was the definition of garrison in Yugoslavia? A location with its immediate environs where units or a unit of the army is deployed, so a garrison is considered to be the whole area where that unit is deployed?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said a garrison normally is referred to as a static, permanent location, whereas the units were deploying into the field, and so maybe I used the word "garrisons," when referring to those incorrectly, but they were large formations in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Can we then take it that in the village of Bukos, where reference was made to the establishment of a permanent garrison, this reference is erroneous?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Bukos probably was an area where there had been a previous garrison. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ciaglinski, I am not answering questions here; I'm asking them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please see 5D26 now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Speaking of Bukos, I'll put to you a daily report of a unit of the Army of Yugoslavia that had frequent and good communication with Mr. Aleksandar Lubarenko [phoen], one of the members of the KVM. Before we see this material, Mr. Ciaglinski, do you know that oftentimes in practice one would receive wrong information and only subsequent insight into the situation on the ground would allow members of the mission to see what was actually going on?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: So are you saying that wrong information was passed to the OSCE headquarters in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: No, I'm speaking in general. Did it happen that you would first receive wrong information, both in the regional centres and the Main Staff in Pristina, in the headquarters in Pristina, and then when you and the other verifiers go out into the field you realise that the situation is quite different?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't say that it was a general situation, but our verifiers were taken from every walk of life and some of them did not know how to interpret what they saw on the ground. We did try and train them. There were only a few experienced people with military know-how, and it's possible -- and it did, I'm sure, happen that often what they thought they saw wasn't quite what had actually happened. And that's why we did follow-up visits.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the registrar now play this exhibit, show us this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: As I said before, Mr. Ciaglinski --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see item 3 on this page. Scroll down a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: It says: "Between 1200 and 1600 hours Mr. Windmar and other gentlemen from the KVM toured Bukos and Brusnik villages and Mr. Lubarenko personally saw that not a single house was torched or destroyed, although they had had information before that everything had been torched." Did you have similar -- did you receive similar information, Mr. Ciaglinski?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't remember this particular report, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you in general. Did such things happen in other situations as well?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No audible response].

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. During the cross-examination by my learned friend Mr. Petrovic you said that the KLA forces built up both their weaponry and troops across a large swath of territory. Do you know that a large number of attacks took place, both against civilians and members of the army and the police while the mission was present in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I suspect you're going to tell me there's an answer missing, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Exactly, Your Honour, you've seen it, 12 through 14, that seems to be all messed up somehow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But let's go back to it once this question's been answered. Can you deal with this question first of all.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, of course there were attacks going on by both sides during our presence in Kosovo, during the mission's presence in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, what was the answer to your previous question? Did such things happen in other situations as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understood correctly the witness said: "If they did," and that was all.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think I actually finished the answer, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, would you care to do so now to complete the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, if these incidents did indeed happen that Mr. Cepic is referring to, I certainly wasn't aware of anything on this scale where something was completely misinterpreted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ciaglinski. Let us just go back to the losses. During the mission's presence in Kosovo, one member of the mission got killed and two were wounded. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was certainly not aware that anyone was killed, not of -- not the -- not of the KVM, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about members of the Kosovo Verification Mission in Srbica. I'll tell you the date when one was killed then two were wounded on the 15th of January, 1999, near Decani, and Mr. Ramush Haradinaj took responsibility for those, which he admitted to you in your interview or conversation on the 20th of January, 1999.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I understand the confusion, and it's one which was cleared up last time, Your Honour. In the Serbian and eastern European translation, often the word "shot" is "killed." And in our language "shot" means possibly wounded, or wounded, while wounded, not necessarily killed. And as I was at this incident throughout the entire time, I know exactly what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: If we're talking about the wounding of these two persons, isn't it true they were wounded by members of the KLA on the 15th of January, 1999? For the record, please.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, to complete the record, are you saying there were three wounded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Only two?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Two members of the mission were wounded near Decani, and before that one was killed in a place called Srbica. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No member of the mission was ever killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Do you know that over 180 persons were killed during the mission's presence in Kosovo, civilians, non-Albanians, Albanians? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly during our time there, that's not true. I believe a lot of our mission members, Albanians who remained, were killed after we left because it's possible that some documents had been left behind which were used by your side to carry out the deeds. But certainly during my time, I was not aware of that, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That may be --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, I wasn't aware that anyone from the mission had actually been killed until the 23rd of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: No, no, I'm talking about citizens, civilians, members of the MUP of the Republic of Serbia, that is the police of Serbia, and members of the Army of Yugoslavia. So while the mission was in Kosovo, exactly 183 citizens of Yugoslavia got killed. Do you know this number?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I accept that number if that's what you say.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: They were killed by the KLA.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you say so. I don't know. But I'm prepared to believe that that's a number which could have been feasible.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Do you also know that as a result of KLA activities and the fact that they took control of large territories another 36 villages were cleansed of Serbs and other non-Albanians while the mission was in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that there was some of that type of cleansing going on by the KLA, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that the KLA, the so-called KLA, intensified its attacks on the eve of negotiations in Paris, that is in addition to the ongoing attacks it intensified them intentionally, additionally?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can confirm that the attacks were intensified, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that the so-called KLA, especially in the area of Nerodimlje and Kacanik, frequently used civilians as human shields?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Sir, in a Prosecution Exhibit P641, which is Appendix DZ8, it says in 4A that KLA brigade commander in the area of Nerodimlje and Kacanik disallowed the evacuation of captured persons which was interpreted by the KVM as an attempt to use these people as live -- as human shields. Does this refresh your memory? This comes from your own mission's report.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... of that report, so I can't remember it, no. I didn't read everything that was published. There was a lot.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. One of the things that you said in your testimony and in your statement and in the Milosevic trial is that you spent quite a bit of time with Colonel Kotur; up to three to four hours a day. You stated that he was an intelligence officer. Do you stand by that assertion, Mr. Ciaglinski, that he was an intelligence officer?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may, I could just expand. I always suspected that he was an officer dealing as part -- or part of special forces just by what he knew, the way he behaved, and what he wore. When I did actually read his transcripts when Mr. Milosevic used him as a witness, where he did actually confirm he was an intelligence officer, as I was, he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: What would you say if I told you that in the Milosevic transcript - and that's an indisputable fact also - Mr. Kotur said that he was not an intelligence officer, that he played a different role. In the Milosevic trial, Mr. Kotur said that he was a chief of infantry.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My learned friend wants to say something.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we have a transcript reference if this is going to be disputable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, I don't have it handy. I need some time to find the reference, but I can find it during the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, you'll shortly have time to do it. You can move on to something else just now.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: You also stated that Mr. Kotur in 1998 and 1999 was responsible for the operations of the VJ in the area of Pec and Djakovica towns. What would you say if I told you that in view of his position and the functions he discharged then, in 1998 and 1999, he was neither authorised or in a position to lead any operations?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I thought I said before the period of 1998 and 1999, because -- I mean, he'd been in Kosovo for most of his career, Colonel Kotur, and he'd been a brigade commander in that area, and that's what I would have been referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Cepic, we'll break there, I think, and you can return to these matters when we resume.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We'll break for about 20 minutes. Mr. Ciaglinski, could you leave with the usher, please, and we'll see you in 20 minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And we'll resume at five past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Before I go back to the topic that we had explored earlier and for reasons of clarity I'd like to refer to Mr. Hannis with regard to what Mr. Kotur stated in the Milosevic trial. The transcript page 47.482, row 23 and 24, Mr. Kotur expressly stated that he was head of the infantry within the Pristina Corps at the time. So much about that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ciaglinski --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The reference has been wrongly transcribed, it should be 47.482. Thank you. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ciaglinski, before the break you said that Mr. Kotur during the period of 1998 was not responsible for operations in the area of Pec and Djakovica, but in your statement dated 2000 in the English version, page 6, paragraph 5, you state verbatim: "Although I never saw Kotur with his unit, it is known to me that during summer 1998 was responsible for the operations of the VJ in Pec and Djakovica." So, Mr. Ciaglinski, contrary to what we heard from you today. Would it be helpful to you if I told you that Mr. Kotur throughout 1998 and in 1999 was head of the infantry in Pristina Corps in Pristina and therefore could not be responsible for the operations as stated by you?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... missing from the quote. I'm looking at page 38, line 25: "Although I never saw Kotur with his unit, it is known to me that during summer 1998 was responsible." I assume there is a pronoun missing. He was responsible?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: He was responsible. [Interpretation] If you allow me, Your Honours, the whole paragraph refers to Mr. Kotur. It's very well stated in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: So if we go back to your statement, Mr. Ciaglinski --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ciaglinski, can you clarify this. In your statement you say what Mr. Cepic has quoted, and I thought you said a bit earlier that you must have been referring to pre-1998 when you said that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I was referring to, Your Honour, was that in the period -- the period 1998/1999 was the period that the OSCE were in Kosovo, and it was a period preceding that, so in the summer of 1998. I stick by what I said, in that he told me he was an officer in the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ciaglinski, isn't it true that on the 20th of March, 1999, you, together with the overall KVM, you left Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Was it the 23rd or the -- I thought it was the 23rd we left.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: On the 20th.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when the -- I left with the entire -- I was with General Drewienkiewicz and Ambassador Walker. We were the last vehicle of the convoy to leave. So on whichever day the KVM left Kosovo, that was the day I left Kosovo. I did not leave before.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: It is the 20th of March, Mr. Ciaglinski, let us clarify that at least. After that, you did not go back to Kosovo before the 13th of June when you returned together with NATO troops as a British officer. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And you could not be aware in great detail with regard to the situation and the developments and the combat between the KLA on the one hand and the Serbian forces on the other, could you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only what I saw in the NATO headquarters and what I heard from refugees who were leaving Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I'm saying this for the following reason. In this courtroom we had head of KLA, Mr. Zyrapi, testifying before this Chamber that -- and who said that fight between the KLA and Serbian forces were conducted in different locations, in different time-frame, from the map that you drew and annotated for us.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it doesn't agree with the information that we were receiving in Skopije.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: As far as NATO headquarters is concerned and your presence there, on Friday in your testimony on page 85, rows from 14 to 19, you stated that sometimes you would be in the intelligence cell of the NATO headquarters and that they could survey TV and radio communications. To the best of your knowledge, how long did the surveillance last, TV and radio communications and telephone communications, in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can tell you because when I was in Kosovo itself it was -- I had no idea in what was happening in terms of communications surveillance because I was not working for NATO. I was part of the OSCE. It wasn't until I actually went to Macedonia and Skopije, then I was just aware of it happening at that time and the comment I made in relation to the Racak orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: So we may infer that during January/February you -- there was surveillance of radio and telephone communications in Kosovo; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how you can infer that, but it's highly likely that GCHQ, our communications centre in the UK, and other organisations, other country's organisations would have monitoring radio traffic communications in the Kosovo area.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Throughout the presence of the KVM in Kosovo; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the course of your testimony and on Friday you mentioned the operation of the army conducted on the Podujevo-Pristina road next to the village of Lebane. Am I right in saying that you reached that place after the operation had started; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You ought to be aware that some actions, and some of which you verified, that were directed against the VJ in the border belt and that were conducted autonomously were in keeping with the high standards. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the Milosevic trial, you stated in parts of your testimony in -- on pages 3174 pages -- lines 31 to 37, that when units were around Podujevo, that recruits were stopped from leaving their units after their expiry of their service. Do you know that the Federal Government was in charge of prolonging the service of recruits because of the escalation of attacks against military units and civil institutions took that decision and not the military. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware of the first part of your statement, but I don't know who made that decision, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, going back a question you said -- or you put the proposition that operations which the witness verified that were directed against the VJ in the border belt were in keeping with the high standards. I take it you mention operations directed by the VJ?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you. This was the proper spirit of that question. I'm sorry that it was taken differently. My intention was to highlight that the VJ conducted themselves and their operations in accordance with the high standards.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Is that right, Mr. Ciaglinski? You have to state it in your microphone because otherwise it's not in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, it was the question and you've clarified it. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a question about the transcript reference. Counsel said page 3174, lines 31 to 37. The lines only go to 25 and I don't see anything on that page referring to Podujevo. Could he double-check for me, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: We've been discussing about different issue right now. About transcript for Milosevic case, it is 3147 page, lines from 7 to 23.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Completely different. Your Honour, if you allow me to continue, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ciaglinski, for the benefit of the transcript, let us make this clear. Isn't it true that the VJ conducted their operations in the border belt in keeping with the high standards, is it true? And you verified some of these operations. Please state your answer into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I answered as you questioned me the first time in the spirit, and I was in the spirit as --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Thank you. Thank you very much. I'm sorry, I interrupted you in false belief that I received a full answer from you, but could you verify yes or no.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was conducted correctly. The answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We've discussed at length the situation in the area of Podujevo, has been mentioned on several occasions, and this most important communication from Podujevo to Pristina, very important for Kosovo; and further on to the administrative border with Serbia. Is it known to you that on the 18th of December KLA members drove 186 Serb families from the town of Podujevo and from the surrounding villages. Is it known to you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: But on the other hand, it is very known to you the incident dated 27th December 1998 when the so-called KLA kidnapped a Serb civilian, Zdravkovic, and with the help of your intervention he was released. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- what I said no to in the previous question was I did not realise it was 186 Serb families and I did not know that they had been driven from the town of Podujevo. I was aware that a number of families had been driven out from the surrounding villages. And the -- your second question was: Yes, I was involved with the release of the civilian Zdravkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I apologise. If I am allowed to go back to the first question. The number of expelled families corresponds to the figure I quoted, and that's 186, to your knowledge.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said I don't know the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. With regard to the incident dated 27th of December when, thanks to your intervention, a Serb civilian was released, you stated also that in that region there was a high concentration of members of the so-called KLA ranging from 1.000 to 2.000 fighters, that they were well armed. Is it correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: What confuses me, Mr. Ciaglinski, is the following. On Friday for the first time you stated, which you failed to state in your previous statements and in the Milosevic trial, that a wounded Albanian was exchanged, who was then taken to a clinic and who later on died from his wounds. This goes for a KLA fighter. Could you explain this difference in your statement and why haven't you stated this in any of your previous statements or testimonies?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think in the initial testimony there was a mention that there was an Albanian rescued as well. I mean, I haven't got the document in front of me, but I'm sure you'll prove me right or wrong in due course. But the reason I didn't mention it was it didn't seem to be of great import because we were talking about the rescue of the Serb and the prevention of conflict. As the situation developed we had to get the Serb out. The only way we could do it was to do a deal. Deals are not unusual in these situations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, I would note it is reflected in his written statement.
