utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you make the reference as to the paragraph in the witness's written statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's page 5 -- 5 of the English, the end of the top paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I can see, this goes for a completely different context. It refers to a wounded MUP and a wounded Albanian, and it is not within the context of the events of the 27th of December. My learned colleague Hannis could correct me if I'm wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It seems, on the face of it, to start with a reference to the 27th of December in the first full paragraph on page 4. However, I suspect that all of this is not really advancing matters very much. It seems a very minor point, a matter of detail that's not really going to be of any significance in the overall context of the evidence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Agreed. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I would briefly go back to the area of Podujevo. On the 27th of -- that we have an abducted Serb who was released with the help of you. On the 26th we have the last Serb killed in Podujevo. You confirmed that at the beginning of your cross-examination. All these events fall in December of 1998, and in the Milosevic trial you said that in the same village of Lapastica, where there was a large stronghold of the KLA where this Serb was abducted, that the -- a physician was killed as well. And my learned colleague tendered a photograph of that event. When this physician was killed and several other persons, you did not -- you were not there, Mr. Ciaglinski, when this happened. Is it correct? You visited a couple of days later to verify the whole incident.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Furthermore, you described a position close to that village, the tank hill, as it's been labelled. Did you know the composition of the unit and its strength on that hillock? Would it be true if I said that one damaged tank was positioned there, one tank damaged by the KLA, while the tank was used in a regular military exercise and that there were some 20 VJ soldiers to secure that tank? Is it correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Is it known to you that on the 20th and between the 20th and 23rd December 1998 VJ exercise was conducted on the Prepolac saddle between Podujevo and Pristina and that the whole elaborate -- or study on that exercise was handed over to the KVM?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Maybe it would jog your memory if I were to mention that upon the return of that unit on the 21st of December, 1998, fire was opened on VJ members injuring three soldiers and damaging the tank that was located on that hill. Do you know of this instant, Mr. Ciaglinski?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The tank on the hill in that position was never damaged; it was a fully operational tank, so I don't know what you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ciaglinski, there are certain reports that Defence is going to tender on the damage of vehicles on that location. Did you mention and notice that the tracks were taken off of that tank and that there were damage -- there was damage by a shoulder-propelled grenade launcher?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I've exhausted my questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Ciaglinski.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cepic. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Actually, Your Honour, at the break I believe Mr. Ackerman asked if he could precede my cross with his own and I've relented.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Colonel, my name is John Ackerman and I represent General Pavkovic. I think I'll be quite brief. You're unique as a witness here because you listen to the questions and answer them, which causes things to move much more rapidly. There's a matter about which I'm confused and which I'm simply going to ask you to help me try to understand. In your statement, it's paragraph 10, if they're numbered consecutively on page 2, you'll know immediately what I'm referring to. You say this: "The role of arms and weapons verification was a complete and utter disaster and was eventually abandoned. We were repeatedly denied permission to access VJ company group positions, barracks or facilities." Now, with regard to your mission in Kosovo you told us on Friday that you basically relied on three documents that you carried around with you; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And in the Milosevic case on page 3142, lines 8 through 12, Milosevic asked you this question: "What kinds of issues were of particular relevance contained in that document to your particular task?" And I think this might have been referring to the Shaun Byrnes document. And you said: "Well, it was very important that the verification went according to the agreements, and therefore we tried to sort of keep both sides to these two documents." Now, would I be correct in assuming you still take the position that it was very important that verification went according to the agreements?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I'm curious about what it means when you say there at the bottom: "We tried to sort of keep both sides to these two documents." When you mean -- what do you mean when you say "both sides"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, although there was no specific mention in the document and nobody from the KLA side signed anything, we did try to maintain some order and peace and prevent the KLA from getting in a position where they would provoke the VJ and the MUP from action. So it was our intention, if you like, it was beyond -- almost beyond what we were asked to do to actually try and maintain law and order and reduce killing to the minimum.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But I think sort of, you know, the language keeping the KLA to these two documents was probably a stretch since they hadn't signed them or agreed to them in any way?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. But as Mr. Hill was trying to get them to agree to something.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that was a pretty laudable thing for him to be doing and I agree with that. The document that you call the Shaun Byrnes document, and that's Exhibit P394, is an agreement between the mission and MUP and has no effect on the VJ, had nothing to do with the VJ, did it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have the document in front of me, but I think it was to do with the MUP positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you would like to look at any document that I refer to, we can certainly make it available to you because I don't want to -- want you to feel like you're being misled in any way. So just tell me if you want to see that document. I can put it up on the screen for you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Would you like to see it? Why are you looking to Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought he might throw a copy over to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Let's put it up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: P394, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm a very trusting person and, you know, it's part of my military training. And if you tell me something, you know, why should I doubt what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to try very hard to live up to that as we go through this.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It says right at the top that it's an understanding between KDOM and the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serbia; in other words, MUP.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Can we move on now? Another document that you -- that you say that you had with you as you moved around was a document which is P395, and this is a document that arose out of a meeting in Belgrade on 25 October 1998, and it bears signatures of Sainovic, Djordjevic, Nauman and General Clark, and perhaps Milosevic. And again, this document - and you can certainly look at it if you want - didn't have any provisions regarding access to VJ company group positions, barracks, or facilities?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. And what you told us yesterday, and was -- the document you actually relied on for such access was -- it was shown to you as P658. It's also in evidence as P432 and that's the agreement on the OSCE-Kosovo Verification Mission; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I'd like to put P432 up on the screen and just look at that document for a moment and -- the page that's relevant is page 3 under specific terms of reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, I think this is essentially the same document as P658, the difference being that this is a copy of the original document with the actual signatures appearing at the end rather than a -- I've lost the English word, rather than a copy of it without the signatures.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And if you look there under specific terms of reference, the paragraph that you were referring to in your testimony yesterday and that you relied on was that first one. "The verification mission will travel throughout Kosovo to verify the maintenance of the cease-fire by all elements. It will investigate reports of cease-fire violations. Mission personnel will have full freedom of movement and access throughout Kosovo at all times." Okay?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, from what I understand and to try and get this all in some kind of perspective, this process all started, did it not, with an agreement between Richard Holbrooke and Slobodan Milosevic to institute a cease-fire in accordance with a resolution of the United Nations numbered 1199. Is that your understanding?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And 1199 we have in evidence as P658, and we can look at it if we want to. Put I'm interested in paragraph 1 of that document, which I think is the first operative paragraph, where the Security Council says: "Demands that all parties, groups, and individuals immediately cease hostilities and maintain a cease-fire in Kosovo, Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, which would enhance the prospects for a meaningful dialogue between the authorities of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the Kosovo Albanian leadership and reduce the risks of a human catastrophe."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, P658 is the agreement in its other form. Does it also contain the United Nations resolution?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No, I have messed up and put down the wrong number. Oh, boy. Now I'm -- I don't know, Your Honour, what number I need. Maybe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, is it vital that the document's on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't think it's vital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, let's proceed and see if we can manage without it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So that that part of the resolution states the demand for a cease-fire, and this is the cease-fire that was basically accepted in Milosevic's agreement with Holbrooke; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And then further down in that document at paragraph 4(B) the Security Council demanded measures to "enable effective and continuous international monitoring in Kosovo by the European Community Monitoring Mission and diplomatic missions accredited to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, including access and complete freedom of movement of such monitors to, from, and within Kosovo unimpeded by government authorities and expeditious issuance of appropriate travel documents to international personnel contributing to the monitoring."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, to interrupt. If I could be of assistance, it's P456, the Security Council Resolution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We'll note that that's the position. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zecevic. I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, we just looked at that paragraph of the verification mission agreement and we saw what it said. And it appears, does it not, to be an effort to -- to put in the agreement what it was that was demanded by the United Nations in that paragraph 4(B) that I just referred you to?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think -- I believe that there -- there is a connection, obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, what the intentions of the drafters were, I don't exactly know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, if we could go back then to P432 and look at that paragraph again, just so we'd have it on the screen as we talk about it. And that's on page 3, under terms of reference, the first paragraph. First of all, as regards access under here, it's clear that the mission is to travel throughout Kosovo to verify the maintenance of the cease-fire by all elements, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. And to carry out that mission it says: "Mission personnel will have full freedom of movement and access throughout Kosovo at all times." Right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Now, there's no other part of that document which specifically provides for access to barracks or facilities of the VJ, is there? You're relying on this language?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Because what else does it mean when it says, you know, full freedom of movement and access?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, let me suggest to you this: The mission is to verify the maintenance of a cease-fire. You don't have to go into barracks, you don't have to go into facilities of the VJ to determine whether they're shooting or not, do you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that the actual -- the full mission was greater than that. It wasn't just to verify the cease-fire. We then talked about organising elections, et cetera. So, you know, I don't agree with you, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I didn't expect you to agree with me. The problem is the document says something different than what you're contending and that's -- and I think that was a dispute that existed from the beginning between your monitoring mission and the Serbian authorities, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: What we said all along about this document, that the document was drafted in haste and the language could have been better. But as it was written, we had freedom of movement and access throughout Kosovo at all times.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But there was a dispute going on between you and the government from the very beginning about whether it had the meaning that you were trying to put on it, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The dispute began the first time we tried to do a verification in the barracks, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And throughout the monitoring mission, that dispute was never resolved, and it was not resolved because the agreement was very vague on this subject and not as specific as, perhaps, you would have wanted it to be. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. I didn't draft it. Greater men than I drafted it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can we take it then from your answer that that dispute was articulated by the Serb side and that explanation given for refusing access?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So if we go back then to your statement, page 2, paragraph 10, where you say: "The role of arms and weapons verification was a complete and utter disaster and was eventually abandoned," there simply was no role of arms and weapons verification; there was simply a role of verification of cease-fire, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe in the -- in amongst the three documents, there was a verification role, besides which a letter was written to Belgrade, to Mr. Milosevic, explaining what we intended to do, to which there was no reply.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, we're talking about agreements here and not just letters that people wrote. And I think the documents speak for themselves and the Tribunal -- the Chamber's going to be able to look at them at their leisure. I want to go to another matter now. I want to ask you if you know of a weapon called a Baret 50-calibre sniper rifle?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And do you know that the KLA had several of those in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Can you tell the Chamber generally about the capabilities of that 50-calibre sniper rifle.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in brief, you can kill someone a mile away.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, the information I have is that it has a range of a couple of miles and can actually destroy an armoured vehicle. Is that wrong?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not wrong, but the operational range -- I mean, most weapons have enormous manufacturer's stated ranges, but the operational effective range is usually less, and this is -- probably a mile is about the correct range for killing someone.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, using a 50-calibre sniper rifle of this magnitude against an individual is kind of an overshot, isn't it? Isn't it more effective against vehicles and things of that nature?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at all. I mean, it's -- at long ranges, this is the weapon of choice of many armies.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. I want to go now to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, was this particular weapon one of those listed by Mr. Zyrapi?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No, it was not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was he asked?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: He was not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It came up in -- it's mentioned in the Milosevic testimony of this witness. He talks about 50-calibre sniper rifle and that got my curiosity and that's how I got to this question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Beginning at paragraph 15 of your statement, which is on page 4, you spoke about incidents in the Podujevo area and I want to talk about Podujevo just for a little while. I assume that when you arrived in Kosovo or before you arrived there you received some briefings about the situation as it existed and had existed before your arrival and the activities of the MUP and the VJ and the KLA?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a very brief outline of what was happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I assume you got some kind of a briefing about the recent history of the Podujevo area or not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not really, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Were you aware that what was going on in that area and had been going on for some time was an effort by the KLA to cut off the Nis-Podujevo-Pristina road and the communication along that road? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And can you tell the Chamber what was the importance of that line of communication?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I mentioned it on the Friday, but it was the main re-supply route and the main transit route, or road route, between Kosovo and the rest of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And so that's why the KLA was making those efforts and it was a continuing effort on their part, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to look at just a couple of exhibits quickly, if we can, 4D82 is the first one. And we just need to see the English version of that. And these documents both predate your arrival, so I don't expect you would have seen them or would know anything about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's the Serbian version. We need the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, what you see here is a 3rd Army command document dated 15 October 1998 addressed to the General Staff of the Yugoslavia army, and it's a regular combat report; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so. I've never seen one before but, yes, I'll take your word for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If we go to page 2, paragraph 4, maybe.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You'll see the language there, the first paragraph under 4, "the situation in the territory," talks about KLA activity going on in the Podujevo area as early as the date of this combat report, does it not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And just while we're on this particular document, I'd like you to look also at paragraph 5.1, and this is 15 October 1997 [sic], and paragraph 5.1 is probably on the next page under the heading "activities." It says: "The commands and units of the army continued with carrying out tasks from the order of the Chief of the General Staff of the VJ," and then it refers to a confidential order and a certain date and so forth. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So it appears, does it not, that the VJ was responding to orders from the Chief of the General Staff at that time, who was General Perisic; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Ackerman, it doesn't seem to me to be a legitimate use of cross-examination to present this witness with these documents. He's answered a very specific question about the situation when he arrived, which is entirely inconsistent, I imagine, with what you're now presenting to him. But bear in mind the discussion we had earlier about the appropriate stage for presenting this kind of evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that, Your Honour. I'm satisfied with what has happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's a translation problem, page 59, 14 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Should 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Should be 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. I want to go to another matter here. At paragraph 45, which is on page 9 of your statement, and this is referred to by Mr. Cepic, that's that situation that you observed on the Podujevo-Pristina road at a place called Lebane, and I'm not going to go back into your language in regards to that, but you spoke about this in the Milosevic trial, and you were asked about it and you said this: "The reason I put this in the statement was to actually show that when the VJ had carried out an operation, they actually performed this within all the legal frameworks and acted humanely and decently, and also performed well as a military unit." Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I now want to look at another document, it's 4D34.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And this is another one of those OSCE-KVM restricted fusion workers -- working papers reports, and this is for a period between 26 February and 4 March of 1999. If you'll look at that first paragraph -- let me just preface it with this. You were shown a number of these reports in the Milosevic case, I know, and on several occasions you said something to the effect that if it's in the report it's probably correct, or something like that. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: This one says: "The KLA appeared to have taken the fight to the Serbs in a number of ambushes and attacks, notably in the Djeneral Jankovic salient, an area previously quiet. To date and in comparison with the activities of the Serb forces in recent months, the VJ has," and the word "been" is probably missing there, "somewhat less aggressive." Are you familiar with that situation at all and would you agree with that analysis?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The problem with working papers is that working papers were not a definitive opinion -- well, a fact -- factual record. I mean, these were working papers where people are trying to come up with some ideal solutions. So when it says that there they were somewhat less aggressive, I don't know. I mean ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, these were people that were on the ground observing the situation that were trying to provide an analysis of what it is they were seeing, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The fusion working papers are actually done by people who were sitting in an office in Pristina, not on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, but based upon what they were learning from people on the ground?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on reports coming in from the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Okay. I want to ask you now about a -- an answer you gave in Milosevic. This is at pages 3285 and 3286. You said this: "Yes, I mean in a conflict, for example, the -- if you are being attacked by terrorist groups, of course a government does have the power and the right to defend itself." And then the question: "And what else did the government do put protect civilians and representatives of the government from terrorists?" Your answer is: "One of the things it did is used disproportionate force on many occasions." Now, can you explain what you mean by the use of "disproportionate force," not in specific incidents, but I hear this a lot and it seems to me that it means when one party to a conflict uses weaponry that's much more advanced than what the other party to the conflict is able to use.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Going back a little bit, when I talk about the VJ, certainly during most of my time in Kosovo and almost until the time we left, almost until we left, the VJ behaved correctly. It was not using excessive force until the last few weeks of March. Now, going back to what I mean by excessive force is if, for example, you have a sniper --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, your word is "disproportionate force." That's what I'm interested in.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Disproportionate force. So if you have a sniper sitting in the window of a house firing at opposition forces to come in with heavy artillery and to wipe out the entire village to kill the sniper I would call disproportionate force.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. How about a few weeks later when NATO was engaged in bombing Serbia with -- by using cruise missiles and cluster bombs and weapons of that sort, would you call that a use of disproportionate force?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I've, you know, sort of -- I can't comment on an operation that I wasn't actually controlling or running. I mean, I don't know what targets you're referring to. Were these empty factories in which there were no people in the evenings, or were they fully manned by personnel?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, you certainly know that the Serbs didn't have cruise missiles and cluster bombs and aircraft like NATO had in any way to --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But you yourself said that, you know, we're talking about, you know, using a more advanced weapons system. And I didn't say using a more advanced weapons system. Disproportionate force to me is just overreacting by completely obliterating a target when the target is minor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. I think that's a fair answer. I have one final question I want to ask you, and I don't know if you know the answer to this or not. I just am curious. In the course of a campaign like NATO was involved in, a bombing campaign basically, which we've seen in Kosovo, we've seen in Iraq, we've seen many places recently, in your experience in the military, the -- the information about targeting, is that information that is widely disseminated or is it closely held? Is it highly secret or not? What do you know about targeting information in terms of the kind of secrecy that is attached to it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's, obviously, secret, and it needs to be kept within a small group; otherwise, you would have things happening like widely reported in NATO when somebody was passing targeting information to the Serbian side at the start of the bombing campaign.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that was happening, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it stopped when action was taken within the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. And the reason that passing that kind of information along is so closely held is, among other things, the danger it provides for the pilots that might be flying those missions?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah. Any other reason?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's just for the entire planning. I mean, if you -- if the enemy were -- are aware of where you're going to hit them, it's not really a surprise. It's not a -- they would clear the area, they would remove their forces, they would remove personnel, or they would sort of go for camouflage and deception and all these sort of things. So, yes, obviously if the enemy knows where you're going to strike him, the enemy will take wise proportions to prevent it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. That's all I have. Thanks very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good day, Colonel Ciaglinski, I am Dan Ivetic, and I am one of the attorneys for General Lukic today, and I am going to have some questions for you. Now, I see from your statement and your testimony here today before this Tribunal that you are a professional soldier. From this can we conclude that you did not at any time but particularly relative to your involvement in the KVM undergo any formal schooling relative to the training and operative knowledge necessary to be an active policeman or police officer?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And am I also correct that you have never been employed as a civilian policeman in any country, have you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now you told us that upon volunteering for the OSCE-Kosovo Verification Mission you underwent some training prior to being deployed on the ground. First of all, about this training, how long did this training last?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: About a week.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And what functions did this training cover? For instance, did your training for the KVM deployment include any training in police procedure and operations, such that you personally would be versed in the police duties, functions, and responsibilities of the MUP of the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And did your training include any element focusing on the structure operations of the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serbia and the laws that were in effect at the time?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, isn't it correct that other people within your mission did in fact receive such training and in fact spent time in the field dealing with the Serbian police, the so-called police verifiers?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, wouldn't you agree with me, sir, that as far as specific appraisals of the Serbian Ministry of the Interior personnel are concerned, you would have to defer to these other individuals within your mission that, (a), had more experience or did receive more extended training in police functions; and (b), spent significant time in the field and had first-hand knowledge of work with the police?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Assuming that the police were carrying out policing-type actions and not army-type actions, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, when you were deployed to the field in Kosovo-Metohija as part of the KVM on the 5th -- on or about the 5th of December, 1998, was the KVM mission at that point in time already in place and functioning, or elements of it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Elements of it were, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And prior to that period of time or prior to the period of time when the KVM mission as a whole came on line, do you know who, if anyone, was undertaking the functioning and the jobs that were later taken up by the KVM?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the KDOM.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The KDOMs, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And the KDOM had been in the area for quite some time at that period. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the French and the American one were, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, were you briefed at any time upon your arrival of the existing security concerns and situations that existed on the territory of Kosovo-Metohija at the time that you were deployed?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean briefed by the Serbian side or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: By the -- by either KDOM or anyone within the KVM.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally wasn't, but people would have been, like my boss, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. You've mentioned a couple times your boss, General Drewienkiewicz, or DZ, as you call him. Do you recall who the personnel were that made up the upper echelons of the hierarchy in KVM mission in Kosovo-Metohija and what their specific duties and responsibilities were?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't go through all of them by name, but I can tell you that obviously Ambassador Walker was in charge and that there were four or five, or thereabout, deputies, one of which -- one of whom was General DZ and the other one was Keller, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would these four or five deputies all be persons who had a higher function than, for instance, yourself within the hierarchy of the KVM?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And specifically when talking about yourself and your role within the hierarchy or the mission, where did you fit in within this hierarchy?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was working directly to DZ, so of middling sort of in the hierarchy.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you have any immediate subordinates that you can recall?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: My job was -- well, if -- yes, because if I was, for example, my job as liaison to the Serbs -- to the commission for cooperation, then I would actually be directly responsible for passing that information to and making sure that the people with similar responsibilities in the regional centres were carrying out their duties in accord with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Am I correct that there were -- I apologise. I have to slow down since we're both speaking English for the interpreters' sake.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Am I correct, then, that there were several individuals who also reported directly to General Drewienkiewicz during the KVM mission in addition to yourself?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, do you recall who the specific communications or liaison officers of the KVM were who were responsible for dealing with the Serbian MUP?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe the person that -- in the KVM headquarters that dealt with them the most -- just -- the name just shot out of my brain. I'm thinking too far ahead. Guy Sans [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And do you recall if Mr. Sans remained in this position the entire time of the KVM's deployment in Kosovo-Metohija?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think for most of the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in your statement you stated that you had limited access to "MUP sites." What are these MUP sites that you're referring to? I mean, are we talking about police stations or ...

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we would never actually -- we were never asked to go and investigate a police station. A police station is a police station. We were more actually interested in deployments of MUP in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So you're -- when you say "MUP sites," is that referring to all or any MUP --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Any deployed MUP in the field, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you would agree with me, I hope, that by the time you arrived in Kosovo-Metohija in December of 1998, the Serbian police maintained so-called observation posts near various roadways per the agreement that we've referred to as the Byrnes agreement and that these observation points were not on the road themselves but were nearby to the road, serving as a security point that did not physically block off the road. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But there were also roadblocks on the road, other ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, when you talk about these other ones, first of all, do you know that at the same time, in addition to these observation points we discussed and the trafficking crime prevention check-points or roadblocks that you mentioned, that these still existed and were used by the MUP outside of Kosovo-Metohija in other parts of Serbia and that they were used by the traffic police in the regular and ordinary course of their duties and functions?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if they were -- I used to travel regularly to Nis and I can't ever remember being stopped by one or seeing one.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in reference to these various deployments out in the field, would you please explain or describe for us what you meant when you used the terminology in your statement of "MUP check-point" in reference to your surprise inspection that you say took place on or about February of 1999?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are the check-points that you referred to earlier yourself, which are the ones not exactly on the road but near the road or in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So are we talking about these observation points or the traffic check-points, since I mentioned both?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're not talking about traffic check-points, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. So we are talking about the observation check-points that were per the Byrnes agreement?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, with respect to this, as you described it, limited access that you had relative to MUP sites or MUP deployments, were -- did you personally eye-witness the denial of access in any of these instances or were you relying upon information sent to you from the field?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I actually organised the event for the inspection to be carried out, and therefore I was trying to coordinate it, and therefore I was personally not going around and looking at these. We had a large number of teams who went out to carry this out.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I was actually asking about the denial of access, since it would appear that with the surprise inspections you did gain access to these deployments. Is it your testimony that as part of this surprise inspection in the early part of 1999 that you were denied access to the observation points that were set forth in the Byrnes agreement?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were denied access to those points, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers kindly make a brief because between questions and answers for the interpreters to be able to follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We got ahead of ourselves there. I'll try and slow down between question and answer. Now, when we talk about this unannounced inspection that you coordinated of all these MUP observation points that you say took place on or about February of 1999, are you certain about this date or is it possible that the inspection was actually carried out in January of 1999?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could have been in January 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, with respect to this inspection, you state that you had confirmed the MUP to be breaching the agreement as to the number of check-points permitted to operate all over the entire territory of Kosovo. Now, in your statement you fail to identify the specific agreement you're talking about. Now, as someone who received -- as someone who was on the ground to verify compliance with several agreements, what particular agreements guided you in terms of making this assessment and organising this inspection of MUP observation points in the field?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was obviously the Byrnes agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, we've already seen that agreement at Exhibit P394 when my colleague cross-examined you. First of all, how about the other agreement signed by Geremek and Foreign Minister Jovanovic, regarding the establishment of the OSCE-KVM mission? Did you in fact consult with that agreement as well while undertaking your inspection?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Because part of the Byrnes agreement and part of the KDOM's future was, I think, discussed in one of the agreements, whereby the KDOM would eventually be absorbed and their work would be absorbed by the OSCE mission. So it was a rolling thing that just rolled into the rest of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: But you would agree with me, I hope, that the Byrnes agreement itself is a one-page document, whereas the KVM agreement signed by Geremek and Jovanovic is a multi-page document that tends to complement each other. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say they certainly do complement each other, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, as part of your surprise inspection of MUP deployments in the field, I believe you mentioned that in addition to the observation points you saw a number of patrols and other deployments. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And you've -- saw this as being a violation of the Byrnes agreement?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I said so at the time, I presume there was a reason why I said it, and I can't remember if patrols were mentioned in the original Byrnes agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, when dealing with either of the Byrnes or the KVM agreement, the Geremek agreement, did you actually take it upon yourself to interpret these agreements or were there staff members of the KVM who interpreted the requirements of the agreements for you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe they were interpreted -- well, I know they were -- it was not my decision. I was too down, too low in the food-chain, if you like. So it would certainly have been agreed with DZ, with certainly Ambassador Walker, so I'm sure these decisions weren't taken lightly. Well, I know they were not taken lightly. And there were legal experts in the KVM itself who would also have been -- and the police also.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's focus, then, for a couple of moments on the Byrnes agreement, first of all, and again that's Exhibit P394, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can have it up on e-court if the witness requires to look at it as I discuss various portions of it. It is one page, so I think we could just have the entire agreement up there at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, would you be surprised to learn that the agreement between Shaun Byrnes and the MUP provides that in determination of increased security concerns, the MUP may increase the number of patrols and utilise armed vehicles on the road where observation points are located using even up to 7.9-millimetre machine-gun armaments on their vehicles and that the only obligation on the part of the MUP is to give notice to KVM. And that's, I believe, subpart 2 of the Byrnes agreement.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir, we have to make sure that our answers are conclusive yes or no. I understand "mm-hmm," but the interpreters may not.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was waiting for you to -- I wasn't actually confirming anything. I was waiting for you to continue because I thought you hadn't finished.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, first -- well, let's limit ourselves to that section for the time being. Are you aware of that -- the existence of that section?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And are you aware of any increased security concerns that were in place in January or February of 1999, since you're not sure when the inspection took place, that the MUP gave notice to KVM of increasing patrols.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was very aware, we all were aware, of the increased security concern. However, I am not aware and -- of any notification given to us because had that been done then we would have known about the actual places to look for these additional points.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm not at this point in time talking about additional points. I'm talking about patrols. Patrols would be mobile, would they not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, patrols would be mobile.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, indeed the Byrnes agreement does not in any way limit the number or frequency of patrols, does it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, if we look further at the Byrnes agreement, we see that the -- if we look at the beginning dealing with the observation points specifically, that at the time this agreement was entered into on the 25th of October, 1998, it was foreseen that the parties would meet subsequently to re-evaluate the number and type of observation points permitted, depending on the changing security situation. That's, I believe, in paragraph 1 of the agreement. Now, did you take any steps to ascertain what the results of any such subsequent discussions between the MUP and Mr. Byrnes or anyone else were prior to conducting your inspection and calling the Serbs in breach some several months later?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We obviously discussed -- we were in constant contact with Mr. Byrnes and he was well aware that we were doing this.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Again, I believe I asked if you had undertaken any steps to ascertain what were the results of the subsequent discussions between the MUP and Mr. Byrnes, his associates, or anyone in the KVM regarding the final number of observation points that were going to be permitted under this agreement.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know nothing about this at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Would that be, again, because you were too low on the food-chain to know about any such discussions?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not necessarily, no. Because I was -- although I was low on the food-chain, I did actually sit next to General DZ and I often had meetings with Shaun Byrnes. I sat in on meetings with the Ambassador Walker, and I tended to know quite a lot of what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, in your statement, in your testimony in Milosevic, and I believe in your testimony here, you have talked about 29 observation points being permitted under the Byrnes agreement. I count fewer than that, based upon the agreement itself. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It certainly looks like it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: 27, is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So it is 27?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And yet would you say that you were the main official at KVM in charge of enforcing this agreement?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's -- I mean, we actually wrote a report which was handed across to General Loncar in which it actually told exactly where we had been, what the points were we actually checked out. It is possible that in my statement when I said 29 check-points, maybe I looked down at the number on the agreement, which is October 29, as opposed to actually giving the correct number, which was 27.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's interesting. We'll get back to that, I think, with some other documents. First of all, let me ask you, you mentioned a report. Would your report, based upon your activities, have been forwarded to your superiors within the KVM as well?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, with respect to your report, at least in your testimony you say it talks about the entire territory of Kosovo and Metohija. Are you aware that this Byrnes agreement, specifically the first part and paragraph 3, limit its application to a -- to a triangle within Kosovo and Metohija, such that the terms of the -- all the terms of the Byrnes agreement do not apply uniformly across the entire territory of Kosovo-Metohija. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: But these are the areas that we actually examined, those points of communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sounds like a good place to interrupt you, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes, that would be fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Another break, Mr. Ciaglinski. If you could leave again --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- please, with the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And we shall resume at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, before the break we were talking about this inspection conducted by the KVM on police deployments on communication routes. Now, we've already heard how you are not specially trained as a police observer or verifier, but based on your limited knowledge or everyday knowledge and common sense, have you ever known the police, any police, when conducting patrols to stop their vehicles to get out and perform their regular duties by way of a traffic or, as we call them, public safety stop?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, focusing specifically upon your inspection that you coordinated as part of the KVM of these police deployments, you have testified that there were a number of sites far in excess of the 29, now that we've seen it's 27, that were permitted under the Byrnes agreement. You say there were almost 40 such sites. Now -- that were manned by the MUP. Now, am I correct that within this number of 40 -- approximately 40 sites, you could be including police patrols that had been parked and traffic check-points that were established for purposes of traffic control or are these all observation points?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was always a major distinction between operational MUP units and the police, traffic police. I don't think I -- or maybe on one occasion I saw real traffic police wearing their little white belts and quite different uniforms to the -- these sort of operational MUP units, and I don't believe that these units were the regular little patrol car with nice friendly policemen with white belts. So that's the answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, are we saying, then, that this number of approximately 40 was exclusively these observation points rather than traffic points or traffic stop points?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there were traffic stop points, but they were not the sort of nice friendly policemen that, you know, have stopped me in the past in the countries I've worked in. These were military-type units.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: This number of 40, though, what is that? Are those observation points or are they traffic points?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's both.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Both. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would ask for the usher to put up Exhibit P432, specifically page 4 of that exhibit on e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And while we're waiting for that document, sir, I would like to ask you if you are aware of the fact that the KVM agreement between the OSCE and the FRY dated 25 October 1998 signed by Mr. Jovanovic and Mr. Geremek, specifically at Article 3, section 3, excludes from the purview of the KVM mission any and all roadblocks established for purposes of traffic and/or crime-fighting concerns. Are you aware of that, sir?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm looking for the paragraph in the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 3; it's right at the top of the screen.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, I see it. Right. That's right. So what we're saying is that if we find them, we report them; which is what we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, if you read there that first sentence even says: "The verification mission will look for and report on roadblocks and other emplacements which influence lines of communication erected for purposes other than traffic or crime control." In fact, the KVM had no authority and no reason to look at traffic or crime control stops erected by the MUP. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: How would you differentiate? They didn't have a big sign saying: This is a crime control stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm asking you, sir, how you differentiated between them since you were the one who coordinated this inspection --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we certainly looked at the -- at the actual output or what these things actually did and how they functioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I believe you testified that you had the Byrnes agreement and this agreement in your pocket at all times.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So therefore you would have knowledge of the fact that no traffic or crime control stop points could be considered a violation of any agreement since they were outside of either of these agreements. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only if you could define what a traffic or crime control stop point was, as I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: May we remind the speakers to make the pause, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... didn't seek to establish the purpose of any particular block, roadblock, that you reported?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I personally wasn't at these particularly sites, sir, so, I mean, it's possible that the people examining them might have asked those questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, your question was actually not in the transcript because the interpreter was speaking at the same time. So I actually didn't even hear the first half of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I simply said that I took it that the witness didn't seek to establish the purpose of any particular roadblock that he reported. And he made the point that he wasn't personally involved in dealing with any.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Can I proceed, Your Honour, or was that -- was there more?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, am I correct that this type of no warning spot check of MUP installations was conducted infrequently, that is to say, that the check you are talking about is the one unique such inspection that KVM undertook of these locations?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was the one coordinated inspection in the areas that were designated. However, the regional centres and the other sort of patrols that would go out would report back if they saw any of these types of roadblocks.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What I'm trying to determine is that in fact this inspection that you're describing, whether it's in January or in February of 1999, that's the only one where in one day all of the 27 observation points were observed by the KVM verifiers?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm going to ask the court officials to put up 6D110 on the e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, as we're waiting for that document what I'm going to be showing you is what purports to be a daily update by the OSCE-KVM dated 6th January 1999 that we received from the Office of the Prosecutor. Now, sir, looking at this document, at least the first page of this document, does this appear to be the format utilised by the OSCE-KVM during the time-period that you were a part of that organisation to report daily events or undertakings?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And before we go further into the document, would it be the standard and regular operating procedures of the KVM mission to include such things as your spot check of the MUP observation points in such a daily update?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to the -- to the organised event of the 27th --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It might be mentioned. I don't know. It was a one-off, so when you say "regular," one is not regular, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, if we can look at section 1 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can scroll down just a little bit more so it's easier. That should be enough right there. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If you can look at developments in the mission area, number 1. First of all, it looks as if this report covers the period of 5 January 1999, and it describes the verification undertaken on that day of all 27 MUP OPs and reports that not all the OPs were manned. First of all, what does MUP OP refer to? Is that the observation points that we've been talking about?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose it must have.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And does this document refresh your recollection as to the fact that the spot check of the MUP observation points was, in fact, conducted in January, specifically January 5th, 1999, and not February of 1999?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fine, whatever you say. If it's written down, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And I guess it's possible the verification 2/99 might have been misinterpreted by you as being February of 1999 if you see in the first line of that statement.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So we're talking about the same event, it would appear; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, we see here that the inspection did not reveal what you have testified to; namely, that of the 27 OPs, not even all 27 of those were found to be manned by the MUP. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And you would not be contradicting the written findings of your own mission, would you? You're not in a position to do that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but I know that there were more than 27 check-points manned.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the report must be somewhere in your files, I presume.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, we'll see about that, sir. Now, taking into account that the document appears to be talking about the inspection, I would ask for -- actually, it doesn't have to be moved. Right at the top of this selection of the document, sir, do you see the preamble to the report that states that: "It appears the MUP and the VJ have stepped up their efforts to restrict freedom of movement in and out of villages. This is probably aimed at providing security for ethnic Serbs during Christmas." Now, taking into account that the Orthodox Christmas falls on January the 7th, and the spot check that you undertook occurred on the 5th of January, you would have to agree that providing extra security during the holidays is, indeed, a normal function of the police in any country, is it not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And that would be especially true if there had been threats or actual attacks undertaken during that same time-period. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't disagree.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, do you recall, sir, that during the same period of time, January of 1999, during the time-period leading up to and during the Serbian Orthodox Christmas, that the findings of the KVM indicated a "province-wide terrorism" affecting the province of Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, do you want an answer from me?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And in fact, I believe that was reported.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let's see exhibit -- Prosecution Exhibit P634, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, this is a report attached to the OTP witness statement of Major General DZ or Drewienkiewicz.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I would direct your attention to the fourth page of this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That should be fine. We're going to need the whole page.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, first of all, I would direct your attention to serial 58 in the middle of the page dated January 5, where it says: "All 27 OPs inspected," and the comment is "most occupied by the MUP."

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Does this refresh your recollection as to whether in fact there is any report about more than 27 observation points being occupied by the MUP on the day of this inspection of all the MUP OPs?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a -- I told you again, I'll repeat it, there was a document produced actually showing exactly where they were that was a KVM document that was passed to the liaison.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, you can't think of any reason why your superior officer would alter your report and report something different than what you reported, can you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only thing that -- from memory -- I can't remember -- did we actually say in the Byrnes agreement, did it actually say that 27 were the actual MUP points that were being -- that was allowed and only so many of those 27 could be manned at any time? I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I was asking you, sir. If you can't remember, I think we're at a loss.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can remember, and I know that more than 27 were occupied.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, sir, you --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were 27 allowed ones plus additional ones that we came across.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, sir, your testimony was that almost 40 were manned and occupied.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in fact the report of your own organisation, at least two reports now that we've gone through, clearly identify that not even the 27 were manned. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: But there were 27 designated ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, if you would consider -- let me ask you this: Would you consider the manning of almost 40 points, in excess of the 27 that is permitted, would you consider that a grave breach of the Byrnes agreement?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it had been -- if we had been warned beforehand about it, then no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you consider grave breaches of the agreement to be chroniclised [sic] in General Drewienkiewicz's summary here, if in fact such a grave breach existed?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The comments are very, very brief, and they don't pretend to sort of be exhaustive and cover all the -- all the points that we're talking about now.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. You indicated that you may not be privy to all the information. Is it possible that if in fact the KVM had received prior notice of other deployments, those deployments would then not be in breach of the agreement and therefore would not be reported in this report or in the other report that we saw.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could that be one of the reasons?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Because we had an agreement about the number of points, and movement around Kosovo was becoming very, very difficult and restricted for everyone, so we wanted to find out how many points were actually being manned, and on that day there were about 40.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we can go down two more lines on this same exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We see the entry for the 7th of January, again the Serbian Orthodox Christmas, and we see there that the KVM notes an identification of trend of unattributable killings, and the comment is "province-wide terrorism." You testified that you recalled this particular instance where the KVM indicated a province-wide terrorism. Was that a province-wide terrorism as a result of KLA activity?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is DZ's abbreviation. I mean, there was terrorism throughout Kosovo, but what does it mean, "province-wide terrorism"? It's as wide as it was broad.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's see what you mean by terrorist actions, because I believe in your direct examination you said that you call a spade a spade, and if you saw a terrorist attack you would label it as such. Now, dealing with armed attacks undertaken by the so-called KLA upon police patrols, this type of activity by the KLA was indeed considered by the Kosovo Verification Mission to be an act of terrorism. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was certainly considered by me to be an act of terrorism and eventually I think accepted by the KVM, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And just to briefly refresh your recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let's have Prosecution Exhibit P638 on e-court. That should be a short document, a press release from the KVM. I believe it consists of two pages. We'll need page 2. Oh, actually, that's the page we need.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, if I can direct your attention to the screen, it would appear that this is a press release regarding a serious breach of the cease-fire near Prizren. And if you look down to the fourth paragraph you see that the KVM -- we just lost it. The fourth paragraph. "The KVM considers that such terrorist attacks and breaches of the cease-fire undermine efforts to reach a political solution of the conflict." And this is dealing with an attack upon two MUP personnel that were witnessed by the KVM administrator. So this indeed shows that the -- it is not just your personal opinion that these attacks were terrorist attacks. The KVM regarded the actions of the KLA as being terrorist attacks. Is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Upon January -- the beginning of January, yes, it was becoming more accepted. Because one of the main talking points at nearly all our meetings with General Loncar and his commission was, you know, what is a terrorist attack and, you know, will we accept that when the KLA have organised attacks that they are terrorist attacks.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What -- what does it matter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, because it depends who's doing the actual fighting, sir. If, for example -- well, who's being attacked. If there's a Serbian action against the village where there are KLA and the KLA are engaged and killed, then that's a legitimate action. If, however, the village is shelled because it might have one gunman in there or someone is said to occupy a house and they shell the whole village, I can't call the entire village or all the villagers terrorists; whereas quite often that would be the actual term used by the Serbian side, that all Albanians were basically regarded as terrorists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I had misunderstood. I thought the preoccupation was with whether you called the KLA terrorists or not, but that wasn't the preoccupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was another issue as well, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
