utterances.text: Okay. Well, what does it matter whether you call them terrorists or anything else, or a liberation army or whatever? Does it matter for our purposes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It didn't matter to us but it mattered to the Serbian side hugely. If we referred to them as a liberation army, they said they are liberating nothing, they are terrorists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, whatever they do is criminal conduct, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, I would like to move just for a moment to your testimony relating to the Racak incident and your recollection of finding out about alleged intercepts of communications between the Serbs after you had left Kosovo and become an officer within the NATO structure again. First of all, sir, with respect to those alleged intercepted communications, am I correct that you yourself did not actually listen to or hear any such intercepts first-hand but were relying upon second-hand information about their existence?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, when did you first hear about the same, about these intercepts?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the very first time it was still in Kosovo -- it's because -- I tried to be very fair to everyone, both sides, and therefore I never accepted things at face value. And I wasn't sure whether Racak was exactly how it was portrayed. And I raised this reservation a few times, and I was basically told by that time in Kosovo that, If you knew the following, would that change your mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Who told you this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: DZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And do you recall when DZ told you that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you talked about the fact that within the NATO structure you heard talk about these communications. Was DZ your source for that as well?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he wasn't. These were the people that actually dealt with intercepts.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And as far as these people talking about these intercepts were concerned, did they talk about the source of their information?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, these things are hugely confidential and classified, and I think they were telling me more than they should anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, as part of the ordinary intel-gathering process employed by NATO, isn't it true that newspapers and news journals are also regularly monitored for obtaining value intel?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I mean, all covert and overt sources are examined.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I presume you were not involved in the gathering of intel relating to these intercepts?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had nothing to do with it at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. So therefore, you have no way of knowing and you cannot exclude the fact that this information about these intercepts may have come from overt sources, i.e., news journals and newspaper accounts of the alleged intercepts, rather than the actual intercepts themselves?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did not ask for any confirmation from my sources in Skopije, but I had no reason to believe that they were telling me lies.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or inventing the facts or repeating facts from newspapers. It's not something the intel world does.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you say that based upon your personal knowledge and experience within the intel world?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's no secret that I was a defence attache in two countries in the former eastern Europe, and I worked very closely with intel agencies.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, we've been talking very generally about these alleged intercepts. Can I conclude from that fact that you have no knowledge or credible information about the identities of the individuals alleged to be engaged in the communications that were alleged to have been intercepted?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we can move on to another topic. As far as the operations of the Kosovo Verification Mission are concerned, am I correct that a great number of your interpreters were, in fact, local Kosovo Albanians?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They certainly were, but mine wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Fair enough. Now, we've heard some testimony here from a Baton Haxhiu, editor of Koha Ditore, that he was utilised as a translator by Jan Kickert and Wolfgang Petritsch when talking to the KLA. Are you familiar with any of these three individuals?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I hadn't met the editor of Koha Ditore, but I was aware of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: How about the other two?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had nothing to do with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. But you are aware of who they are?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've heard their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, during his testimony, Mr. Haxhiu testified that in fact he deliberately mistranslated what the KLA was telling these western observers so as to tone down the message and make it more palatable for western ears. Did you in fact have any knowledge or experience that the information western observers in Kosovo were hearing from Albanian translators was in fact doctored or misrepresented in such fashion?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was certainly aware that occasionally my own Serbian interpreter, when the discussions were getting quite heated, would actually tone down the whole conversation, the interpretation, so as to avoid any further sort of unpleasantness than I was involved in with the work. So I wouldn't -- I mean, certainly the Albanian interpreters, at times also to -- if they were talking with KLA, discussions would be heated as well, and so I am sure there are occasions when the interpreters would have toned down what they were saying. It happened to me, I know, with my Serbian interpreters, and it probably happened to the Albanian interpreters working with the KLA -- with our people, conversing with the KLA. I mean, I had experiences of dealing with Rahman, and he was holding a gun to my head. And so the interpreter was, you know, very careful what he said at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You would agree with me, would you not, that this possibility could provide for some serious concerns as to some of the critical information being provided to field operatives of the KVM?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the gist was usually correct. You know, it's -- I'm an interpreter myself of a couple of languages and I know how difficult it is to get it exactly right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we can move on to another issue within the KVM. Is it correct that William Walker and others around him, particularly my fellow Americans in the mission, appeared to have a different agenda from the rest of the mission, namely that they were sent there by the State Department to remove Milosevic at all costs?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: How could I possibly know this?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, did you hear anything within the hierarchy of the KVM that you were involved in, anything from DZ, for instance?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nothing from DZ, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, possibly after the whole thing was over, during the last few years, there have been many discussions about what the hidden agendas of various nations were.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you recall any event or discussion wherein Mr. Walker tried to veto a report about wounded MUP personnel and kidnapped VJ soldiers that General Drewienkiewicz wanted to forward along and that General Drewienkiewicz had to override Ambassador Walker based upon a majority vote of the other members of the upper echelons of the KVM hierarchy?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the specific event, but I can tell you that quite often the -- the immediate information you received after an incident was so confused, it was better to wait a bit and wait until the whole thing had actually crystallised. So, for example, in my own incident in Decani when I was attacked, everybody assumed it had been the Serbs who had actually attacked us for some reason, and that was going to be the report that was being sent back to our capitals, but I was quite adamant and trying to stop this because I didn't believe it was true. And as it happened it wasn't the Serbs; it was the KLA. It's very difficult to get the right interpretation straight away.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, my question for you is aimed at the inter-workings of the KVM hierarchy. Do you recall that there was a sharp division between the hierarchy such that in this instance that I've referenced General DZ had to take a poll or vote amongst the top members and the majority rather than everybody agreed to send a report along and then that report was sent?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember this particular incident, but I can tell you that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's a good enough answer. The question has already been answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, if we can look at -- well, first of all, am I correct that the KVM mission had a department for analytical assessments that essentially was the intelligence arm of that organisation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've already mentioned, it was called the fusion centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, do you recall the fusion centre reaching a conclusion or finding that the KLA was expected to fabricate incidents and even carry out killings of Albanian civilians in order to ascribe the deeds to the MUP and the Yugoslav army?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we examined all sorts of possibilities. This could have been quite easily discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can have Exhibit 6D109 on the screen. The English version for the witness and for the Court, I believe, would suffice.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, this is a document that we've received --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And for the Court's information, this is a draft translation from the OTP. So this document at this point in time is being tendered pursuant to identification, and we'll need to get an official translation, I think, before it's accepted fully as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you not happy with the OTP translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I am happy with it, but I don't know what the Court's standing order or rule on that would be, if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, unless Mr. Hannis objects to this being accepted as a translation, it seems appropriate to me to accept it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have no objection at this time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, this is the minutes on which a meeting between Mr. Nikolaev of the KVM mission and the Yugoslav Ministry of Foreign Affairs dated January 12, 1999. Now, if we look at item number 3 here it -- first of all, do you recall Mr. Nikolaev and what his position within the KVM was?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he was a reconstruction man.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, we see here that in item 3 the minutes detail Mr. Nikolaev giving a briefing of the assessment conducted by the department for analytical assessments on the KLA?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I think the part that we want is actually on the next page, the top thereof.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Where the minutes, at least, describe Mr. Nikolaev as talking --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We can scroll down a little bit more. A little bit more. There -- right there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The second bullet point from the bottom where it says: "The KLA is expected to fabricate incidents, and even carry out killings of Albanians in order to ascribe the deeds to MUP and Yugoslav army personnel." Does that refresh your recollection as to whether in fact this particular conclusion or finding was in fact one reached by the KVM department for analytical analysis, the fusion centre?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly we discussed these, every single possibility and this certainly was a possibility that they might participate in. And if you're trying to look for discrepancies between the opinions of the higher echelons of the KVM, I think it is rather good that it was open to debate, that not everyone sang from the same hymn sheet, that, you know, we would look at it, discuss it, take a vote on it, if necessary, and move forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Were you a part of the vote undertaken among the deputies of the KVM mission?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So your position was not that high up on the hierarchy, the overall hierarchy?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I've said this before.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, we have already looked at one fusion report -- one fusion centre report. My colleague, Mr. Ackerman, that's Exhibit 4D34. I'd like to return to it for just a moment to highlight some points that were not discussed. I believe this is a multi-page document. We'll start at the first page. Sir, were you one of the individuals within the KVM hierarchy who was privy to such restricted information as the KVM fusion working papers?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. So you would be familiar with this type of document. Now, looking at --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not read all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't expect that you would remember all of them if you had read them all after this period of time. But looking at this first page of this fusion working paper, first of all, the summary at the beginning, which is a little bit blurry on the screen, but it talks about Djeneral Jankovic, and in summary it talks about 100 KLA that crossed over from Macedonia to the Djeneral Jankovic area that joined with the local militia and then encouraged the locals to leave and how this event had been misreported as a Serb massacre. Now, does this -- do you recall this event, first of all?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And do you recall any other events wherein KLA activities, i.e., forcing people to leave, were -- or attempted to be utilised by the KLA to try to pin the blame upon the Serb forces, either the MUP or the VJ?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not off the top of my head, no, but I'm sure you'll remind me in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we look at -- well, pages 4 and 5 of this report we don't, I don't think, need to go to them, talk about the KVM assessment that the ethnic Albanians will continue to work on international sympathy for their cause, and therefore KVM staff are being warned to expect movements of large amounts of people at the orders of the KLA for maximum media exposure of displacement. Do you recall receiving such instructions or warnings from KVM or were you involved in perhaps giving such warnings to the KVM officials in the field?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because as I said, my major function was to liaise with the Serbian authorities and to facilitate our people in the field to be able to visit and go around the field. I was not dealing with the KLA. And we did this specifically so that I wasn't then accused of passing information between the two or even endangering myself by knowing something that the other side might want to find out from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, this document does not deal in fact in the areas you've been exploring. Now, we've had this witness for some considerable time. A very wide range of issues have been explored. Is there anything of direct relevance to your case that you now have to deal with?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, there is, Your Honour. I've got several areas that I'm trying to hit because of course this witness has been used to introduce a large number of these KVM documents and in fact was initially proposed as a three-hour Rule 92 ter witness and so I do have areas and I'm trying to go through them as fast as I can with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, at the moment, as I say, we're not dealing with fact. What is the next subject you have to deal with?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The next subject I have to deal with is with respect to the reports of two other KVM individuals who operated with the Serbian MUP, who were police verifiers, one was, and the other was a KLA verifier who have accounts of things that I would like to ask this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And do these challenge what this witness has said?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm going to find out whether they challenge what he said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You must know whether they challenge what he has said so far.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: He has not, I believe, testified to -- they do contradict what he has said in his statement, yes, as far as the actions of the MUP and the access to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that's the sort of thing I would expect you to be concentrating on in view of the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right. Well, I can -- as I said, that was my next area. I can move along to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, we earlier talked about deferring to persons with more mission-specific training and who were in the field. I would like to ask you about two individuals who were in the KVM. First of all, are you familiar with Captain Roland Keith, a 32-year veteran of the Canadian Armed Forces and a police verifier with the KVM?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the name rings a bell.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And how about Christopher John Clark, a 16-year veteran of the British Army, seconded to the KVM in October of 1998 and one of the operations officers responsible for management and coordination of field patrols?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know him very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, before we go on to these two individuals and what they had to say about their experience in the KVM, are you familiar with the fact that in addition to holding most of the villages surrounding the town of Glogovac, the KLA had a command headquarters in the village called Gornje Obrinje?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where they had their headquarters because I -- after my first few weeks I decided I would not go to any of their headquarters in case I accidentally mentioned some of my meetings with my Serbian colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right. Well, we'd like to then have Exhibit 6D106 up on the screen, and I'll try and short circuit the questioning on this by directing you to page 7 of the document. This is the OTP witness statement of Christopher John Clark, one of the KVM verifiers, who was with the -- who was observing the KLA. And at this page, sir, he indicates that if the KVM wanted to speak with the General Staff of the KLA, they went to Gornje Obrinje, because that's where they could find them. You have nothing to contradict Mr. Clark and would in fact defer to him as being someone who was with the KLA as you were not. Is that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Don't answer that question. Mr. Ivetic, this is not a challenge to this witness's evidence. It's something about which he has said clearly he has no knowledge. Now I'm expecting you at this stage in this cross-examination to be dealing with matters which are directly challenging the witness and necessary for your case, because this can all be presented in the Defence case.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, is it your testimony that the Serbian MUP observation points and check-points that were established were not operated in such a way to be the normal functioning of the police, that there was some kind of ulterior or negative operation of these deployments?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of the MUP in Kosovo operated, as I said, not in the police fashion but in the military fashion, and that was the major difference. It was a function that I certainly wasn't so conscious of in any countries that I worked in, and it wasn't the sort of duties that the police in most countries that I know of operate in.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, are -- is it your testimony that there were -- that there was any abuse at any check-points -- at all the check-points that were operated by the Serbian MUP?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure that there were instances of abuse of personnel, locals, making it difficult for our own patrols to operate as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You don't have any first-hand knowledge of any such allegations, do you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Reports were being made every single day. I was reading. There were just so many that I -- it's not something that I carry around in my head.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right. Well, if Captain Roland, on the one hand, at page 33460 of his testimony in the Milosevic case, lines 1 through 12, said that he personally observed a number of these operations in progress and that it was his observation that there was not any abuse or physical harm to any inhabitants conducting lawful business who transited these Serbian police check-points, you would have to defer to him and the other individuals on the ground, would you not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose the actual killer phrase there is "lawful business." I mean, who defined what lawful business was?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, I take it that the KVM verifiers on the ground would have to define what they were seeing based upon their experience and knowledge. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I'm sure that they did this and this is Captain Roland's interpretation. It's one person.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, with respect to your testimony that in fact there were -- there was a denial of access and problems with obtaining cooperation from the Serbian MUP, again the testimony of Roland Keith states at page 33465, lines 15 through 20 of the Milosevic case, that in his area of responsibility he regularly dealt with the Serbian police stations in Kosovo Polje and Obilic, for instance, and was received hospitably and professionally by the Serbian police, and at all times they cooperated with all his requests and he was not obstructed in any way from carrying out any of his duties or responsibilities by them. Now, did you in fact receive reports from this individual and others in the course of your deployment with KVM to show that, in fact, the Serbian police stations were cooperating with the KVM observers?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, from my own experience, I sort of would go along with that completely. I didn't say we had problems with police stations; I said we had problems with deployed units.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, is it correct that during the time-period from October through February of 1999, when there was this tension and this campaign of terrorism, that in fact the KVM reporters on the ground reported back up the chain to you and to the other parts of the KVM hierarchy that while the -- while the Serbs were generally adhering to the cease-fire and other agreements, the KLA was not and was in fact being quite provocative?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would -- in general I would say that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you specifically recall a meeting on the 5th of January -- on the 5th of March, 1999, with a Lieutenant-Colonel Adamovic of the MUP, wherein you expressly said that same point to Mr. Adamovic? And that the international community was losing patience with the KLA, whereas the police were showing restraint?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I just answered that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Now, throughout his testimony, which is, I believe, Exhibit 6D113, Captain Roland of the KVM commented on the regular and altogether normal police duties being performed by the Serbian MUP, for instance, transcript page 33490 of the Milosevic proceedings. Now, you have testified in the Milosevic case that the MUP was not carrying out ordinary policing duties and were not out in the streets preventing crime and traffic, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a foundation objection about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We don't know where Captain Roland was, what part of Kosovo he was in, where he was working, how many events he saw, and without that information I don't think it's an appropriate way to cross-examine this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well -- yeah. Mr. Ivetic, it doesn't seem to me proper cross-examination at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm trying to short circuit this because of the shortness of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're just using up time unnecessarily. It's not making any real progress at all on this. You can call Roland Keith in your own case and make all these points.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We intend to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, please do. But let's move on to something that this witness can speak directly about and with authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, let's turn to the appearance and armament of the MUP that you saw in Kosovo. Now, from your testimony and in your statement, it would seem that you are surprised by the fact that the police were utilising long-barrelled rifles. Is that correct? That they were armed with long-barrelled weapons, in addition to short-barrelled side-arms?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I suppose your training for the KVM mission did not include the historical fact that since World War II, not only the Serbian police but in fact the police of all the republics covering the territories of the former Yugoslavia were armed with long-barrelled weapons and not just side-arms, including assault rifles, and this extended even to traffic policemen? Am I correct that you did not have this covered in your training?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have also worked in eastern Europe, and I worked in Berlin in the 1980s, and East Berlin, where I was very aware of how these things were done. And normally -- only very abnormally would the police openly go around with long-barrelled weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did your previous experience include the former Yugoslavia, which is what I was limiting my question to?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, on the topic of the appearance of police you state in your statement that unit affiliation would be difficult at times because the insignia would be removed. Now, despite this assertion you could always plainly identify a police officer or a police member, I should say rather than officer, so there's no confusion, policemen, because of the presence of the remaining markings on the uniform or the webbing of the uniform. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know what the VJ army wore and how they looked, and these people were not VJ army. So if you're saying they were not policemen, then what were they?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No, what I'm saying is with respect to policemen, sir, would you agree with me that if you were close enough to discern that a uniform is camouflaged, either camouflage green or blue. At that point in time you can easily discern whether someone is police or not due to the visible police emblems, insignia, and markings on the uniform, the vest, or webbing as it's called. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you could get close enough, possibly, if they had the insignia on. They didn't always have it on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Isn't it a fact that the webbing always had the insignia on?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm being told to slow down.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do read Cyrillic, and even if it wasn't Cyrillic, then I would recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That was my point, that it's on the uniform, the Cyrillic lettering?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it was there, then I would recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, from what I recall of your previous testimony you confirmed that the Serbian police did not have their own tanks but did have blue armoured personnel carriers. Am I correct that there were occasions known of to you where the KVM personnel wherein the KLA captured MUP vehicles and then used them in their combat operations?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It happened very infrequently. I think there was an occasion where there was a captured MUP vehicle and it was used by the KLA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The transcript has wrongly attributed the capturing to the MUP. I think the question was where the KLA captured the MUP vehicles and used them in operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That is correct. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And do you recall in the incident that you are talking about whether in fact the captured MUP vehicle was then utilised by the KLA in combat activities?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Then I don't think we need to go to 6D106, which talks about that at page 12. Now, based upon your knowledge and experience from the KVM and the reports that were sent to the KVM, even though you were not with -- you were not charged with observing the KLA, did you have knowledge of the fact that the KLA had an internal security force specifically responsible for conducting acts of retribution against the local Albanian and Serbian populations?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Don't answer that again. Mr. Ivetic, please concentrate on matters that you know this witness will be able to deal with. You have not got complete freedom so far as time is concerned, and I don't think you're exercising your use of time responsibly at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, the Prosecution has introduced thousands of pages of exhibits with this witness that I'm sure are -- he has just as little or maybe just as much knowledge as he does of my questions that I'm asking him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, I wasn't aware that they had introduced thousands of pages of exhibits. And if that is the case, then I will change my approach to this. Thousands of pages?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I don't know the exact number but it's a significant amount of pages with respect to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thousands of pages, Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I don't know the exact number, Your Honour. I may have misspoken about the exact number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think you may be well out of order in that comment. Now let's be realistic about this, otherwise we're going to have to have a Status Conference soon and look at the whole issue of the use of time. As counsel, your team has been the one who -- which has made far more use of time than anyone else so far. That's going to have to be reviewed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, the witnesses have also spoken quite -- in detail about the activities of the Serbian police, and as the only defendants who have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, indeed that's the case, but there are occasions when you have to exercise restraint. You've to look at everybody's interests. You've been given a very free hand up until now. But at the moment you're not demonstrating a responsible approach to this and you will have to change that quickly, otherwise I'll bring your cross-examination to an end.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right. I will move on then specifically to questions relating to the MUP staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, you stated, I believe, that you visited Colonel Mijatovic of the MUP on at least ten or more than ten occasions. Isn't it correct that despite your claim that Mijatovic rarely came to the meetings with you and with Loncar that in fact Colonel Mijatovic met every single day with the KVM personnel specifically assigned as liaisons for the MUP, the staff of Mr. Guy Sans and the other KVM persons charged with MUP liaisons?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible that these meetings took place. As I understand, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you talk of the MUP building where Mr. Lukic and Mr. Mijatovic were based as being a command structure with a huge antenna. Now, am I correct that when you returned to Pristina after KFOR moved in, this building had been -- had been bombed by NATO?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in fact the building had been evacuated prior to the bombing and that in fact it was bombed on the 24th of March and was unused and empty from the 24th of March onwards?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let me ask you, do you have a basis of -- do you solid information about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About what, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: About this question you've just been asked, about the circumstances in which that building came to be bombed and who was in it at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew who was in it -- during my time in Kosovo, that's where I would have meetings with Mijatovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Indeed. But you're being asked about when you returned to Pristina and you learned that it had been bombed, and you're now being asked if you knew it had been evacuated prior to the bombing and the date of the bombing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I mean, Mr. Ivetic, this is most unreasonable, and I want now a list of the subjects that you're about to cross-examine on before I make a final decision on bringing this to an end.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: These are quite unnecessary questions to pose to this witness and a complete waste of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I respectfully disagree, Your Honour. I am talking about -- first of all, I have the topic of the burning documents that he testified to when he returned to Pristina, which is the area -- one of the areas I'm going into now, and then his specific testimony relative to interactions with Mr. Lukic and the structure of the MUP staff. And those are the areas that I have to complete.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, there are plainly very important matters yet to be covered, and hopefully briefly, but you have run the risk, a serious risk, of prejudicing your own client's interests by the way in which you've conducted this cross-examination, by not prioritising your cross-examination at all. Tell me why you needed to ask that question of this witness about the bombing of the building in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It's very important --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The bombing may be important. But why did you have to ask this witness about it?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It's important to set the ground work for his observations of documents being removed from that building and being burned and when those documents would have been the building in the first place and if they --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If it was that building.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If it was that building, correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And that's your position that it is that building, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, I was going to ask him because it's my understanding that there is a three-building compound that was occupied by the MUP -- the SUP of Pristina, the MUP staff, and this would be the building that was being vacated pursuant to the Kumanovo agreements for the KVM to take over, and as part of the Kumanovo agreements all the documents and the archives in that building were to be removed and to be disposed of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, what was the relevance to these issues of when the bombing took place and whether there were personnel in the building at the time?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The fact that it is trying -- the Prosecution is trying to assert that these burning documents are in fact identity documents being destroyed of persons that are relevant to the indictment, when in fact these documents would have been in the building prior to any of the events in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that. But answer me the question I've just asked you, which is: What is the relevance of the date of the bombing and whether there were personnel in the building when the bombing took place, bearing in mind that it's three months before the witness's return to see this event.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It would set the time-period for when the building was vacated. The building was vacated prior to -- the building was vacated while the OSCE was removing itself from Kosovo, and now the witness testified previously that he left on March the 24th. I think now he's changed that testimony to being sometime prior to March the 24th, but I really don't know when he left. There were OSCE verifiers that did leave after --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're now trying to confuse the issue because plainly the events that you're about to raise occurred long after the 24th of March. Anyway, that's -- concludes our proceedings now for today, but we are now faced with a difficulty in programming evidence, and that difficulty we are going to have to address. But that's something we have to reflect upon. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have a scheduling difficulty I have to bring to the attention of the Court and Defence counsel. Mr. Brunborg, our demographics expert, is -- was scheduled to testify Wednesday. We have two additional witnesses between this witness and him. But I would propose to do what we've done in past weeks and take a break from wherever we are, put Mr. Brunborg on Wednesday and complete him and then resume.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, thank you, Mr. Hannis, for alerting us to that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters would like to note that we've been having enormous difficulties today with the speed of the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Ciaglinski, we have to break there for the evening. We will see you again tomorrow afternoon. Meanwhile, please no discussion with anyone at all about any aspect of your evidence at all, and return to resume at 2.15 tomorrow afternoon. Can you now leave the courtroom with the usher, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And we will resume at 2.15 tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 21st day of November, 2006, at 2.15 p.m. 18 19 20 21 22 23

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.05 p.m.,
